Reading guide

This monograph develops a precise question: how much of a relation structure can be recovered from integer-height populations, and where does its first hidden difference appear in arithmetic? Chapters 1-4 establish the objects and finite observation hierarchy. Chapters 5-8 develop primewise assembly, local analytic comparison and singular synchronization. Chapters 9-11 give exact examples, inverse questions and the bridges to earlier work. Chapters 12-14 develop computational methodology, the research program and the literature. The implementation appendix states what version 0.1.0 actually executes. The final roadmap defines thirty-six subsequent development pushes.

The central distinction is between an observation and the correspondence it forgets. A binary census can agree for every subset size and boundary size while a nested-height census differs. The arithmetic lift retains these local distinctions and turns the first discrepancy into a controlled ratio singularity. It adds analytic structure rather than new graph information. The full marked hierarchy explicitly contains the binary sector; complete graph reconstruction remains a research question.

Definitions and theorems are supplied with hypotheses and proofs. Finite graph calculations have explicit inputs and independently replayable outputs. Established antecedents are attributed in the literature chapter and bibliography. The book is a research foundation and executable companion, not a claim of a completed priority search or unrestricted reconstruction.

1 What the population observes

1.1 A relation before a prediction

This book begins with a finite graph and a deliberately restricted experiment. Each vertex receives a nonnegative integer height. An edge pays the square of the difference between its endpoint heights. We count all height assignments having a specified total height and a specified energy. We then ask how much of the original relation between vertices survives in those counts. The question concerns the information contained in an exact mathematical observation. It does not require interpreting vertices as people, particles, assets, or physical locations.

The restriction is essential. If an experiment reports every vertex height and every labeled edge contribution, the graph can be read directly from the report. The interesting problem begins after that correspondence is removed. A histogram may tell us how many assignments have a certain energy without telling us which assignments they were. The resulting observation can preserve information that a familiar spectrum loses, while still losing information of its own. Establishing either possibility requires a proof or a concrete exact comparison.

There are consequently two distinct tasks. The forward task computes the population produced by a supplied graph. The inverse task decides what a population determines about its source. An efficient and correct forward computation does not settle the inverse question. Nor does a pair of distinguishable examples establish that every pair is distinguishable. Throughout the manuscript, reconstruction is a question to investigate, not an advertised theorem.

1.2 Objects, assignments, and the meaning of a coefficient

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a finite simple undirected graph with labeled vertex set V={0,1,…,k−1},k≥1. V=\{0,1,\ldots,k-1\},\qquad k\ge1. An edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices, and each unordered pair occurs at most once. Write did_i for the degree of vertex ii, and Aij∈{0,1}A_{ij}\in\{0,1\} for the adjacency matrix. Connectedness will be required explicitly when needed. The basic formal counting series itself is defined for disconnected graphs as well.

A height profile is a vector a=(a0,…,ak−1)∈ℤ≥0ka=(a_0,\ldots,a_{k-1})\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^k. Its volume, energy, and span are |a|=∑iai,EG(a)=∑{i,j}∈E(ai−aj)2,h(a)=maxiai−miniai. |a|=\sum_i a_i,\qquad E_G(a)=\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}(a_i-a_j)^2,\qquad h(a)=\max_i a_i-\min_i a_i. The word volume always means total integer height. It is not a Euclidean volume, a determinant, the number of occupied vertices, or the number of nonzero levels. A profile of volume four might put height four at one vertex, height two at two vertices, or height one at four vertices. These assignments generally have different energies.

Define the local series LG(x,q)=∑a∈ℤ≥0kx|a|qEG(a)=∑m≥0CG,m(q)xm. L_G(x,q)=\sum_{a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^k}x^{|a|}q^{E_G(a)} =\sum_{m\ge0}C_{G,m}(q)x^m. The coefficient [xmqe]LG[x^m q^e]L_G is the number of original labeled assignments of volume mm and energy ee. It does not count graph automorphism orbits. If a symmetry exchanges two assignments, both remain in the population. This convention makes coefficients directly comparable to enumeration and avoids inserting unannounced symmetry factors.

Theorem SNG-F01 (finite local coefficients). For every finite graph on k≥1k\ge1 vertices and every m≥0m\ge0, CG,m(q)C_{G,m}(q) is a polynomial in qq with nonnegative integer coefficients. Its coefficient sum is CG,m(1)=(m+k−1k−1). C_{G,m}(1)=\binom{m+k-1}{k-1}. If Δ=maxidi\Delta=\max_i d_i, its degree is at most Δm2\Delta m^2.

Proof. The nonnegative integer solutions of a0+⋯+ak−1=ma_0+\cdots+a_{k-1}=m are the weak compositions of mm into kk parts. The usual separator construction gives their number as the displayed binomial coefficient. In particular, there are finitely many terms in CG,mC_{G,m}. Every energy is a nonnegative integer. Moreover, $$ E_G(a)=\sum_i d_i a_i^2-2\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}a_i a_j \le\Delta\sum_i a_i^2\le\Delta\Bigl(\sum_i a_i\Bigr)^2. $$ The first inequality uses nonnegativity of all heights; the second follows by expanding the square. This proves all assertions. ▫\square

Thus LGL_G is well defined as an element of ℤ[q][[x]]\mathbb Z[q][[x]]. This assertion is formal: no choice of numerical xx or qq, and no convergence argument, is required. Later analytic interpretations must separately state the region in which a formal identity can be evaluated.

1.3 Removing a repetition that carries no relational information

Adding the same integer to every height leaves every edge difference unchanged: EG(a+t𝟏)=EG(a),|a+t𝟏|=|a|+kt. E_G(a+t\mathbf1)=E_G(a),\qquad |a+t\mathbf1|=|a|+kt. Every nonnegative profile has a unique decomposition a=b+t𝟏,t=miniai,minibi=0. a=b+t\mathbf1,\qquad t=\min_i a_i,\qquad \min_i b_i=0. We therefore retain the normalized series BG(x,q)=∑b≥0minb=0x|b|qEG(b). B_G(x,q)=\sum_{\substack{b\ge0\\\min b=0}}x^{|b|}q^{E_G(b)}. The normalization removes the common-height tower, not an assignment-specific ambiguity. It retains one explicitly specified representative of each integer profile modulo common translation.

To distinguish assignments with one nonzero level from assignments with several levels, introduce the full marked series ℬG(x,q,z)=∑b≥0minb=0x|b|qEG(b)zmaxb. \mathcal B_G(x,q,z) =\sum_{\substack{b\ge0\\\min b=0}} x^{|b|}q^{E_G(b)}z^{\max b}. The symbol BG(x,q,z)B_G(x,q,z) may be used for this same three-variable object when its arguments are displayed. In these foundational chapters, ℬG\mathcal B_G makes the extra mark visually explicit, while BG(x,q)=ℬG(x,q,1)B_G(x,q)=\mathcal B_G(x,q,1). On normalized profiles, maximum height equals span. Consequently zz records a property that common translation does not change.

Theorem SNG-F02 (normalization and span marking). For every finite graph on k≥1k\ge1 vertices, BG(x,q)=(1−xk)LG(x,q). B_G(x,q)=(1-x^k)L_G(x,q). More generally, if L̃G(x,q,z)=∑a≥0x|a|qEG(a)zh(a), \widetilde L_G(x,q,z)=\sum_{a\ge0}x^{|a|}q^{E_G(a)}z^{h(a)}, then ℬG(x,q,z)=(1−xk)L̃G(x,q,z). \mathcal B_G(x,q,z)=(1-x^k)\widetilde L_G(x,q,z). Both normalized series have nonnegative integer coefficients despite the subtraction in these formulas.

Proof. Use the unique decomposition a=b+t𝟏a=b+t\mathbf1. Energy and span are unchanged, whereas volume increases by ktkt. Hence L̃G=ℬG∑t≥0xkt=ℬG/(1−xk)\widetilde L_G=\mathcal B_G\sum_{t\ge0}x^{kt}=\mathcal B_G/(1-x^k). Specializing z=1z=1 gives the first identity. Each coefficient of ℬG\mathcal B_G counts an explicitly defined finite set, proving nonnegativity without relying on cancellation. ▫\square

Keeping kk fixed, BGB_G and LGL_G contain exactly the same formal information: either is recovered from the other by multiplication or division by 1−xk1-x^k. The span mark is a different matter. Specializing z=1z=1 merges populations of different spans. We do not assume that this merging can be inverted.

Observation Coefficient meaning Correspondence deliberately removed
LG(x,q)L_G(x,q) All profiles by total height and energy Identity of each profile
BG(x,q)B_G(x,q) Translation-normalized profiles by total height and energy Identity of each normalized profile
ℬG(x,q,z)\mathcal B_G(x,q,z) Normalized profiles by total height, energy, and span Identity of each profile within a marked cell
[z]ℬG[z]\mathcal B_G Binary profiles, excluding the two constant profiles Identity of the vertex subset
BG(1,q)B_G(1,q), when defined Translation classes by energy alone Total height and span

1.4 Labeled populations can define unlabeled observations

Labels specify the population being counted, but the aggregate series does not privilege a particular labeling. Let σ:V(G)→V(H)\sigma:V(G)\to V(H) be a graph isomorphism. Transport a profile by a′σ(i)=aia'_{\sigma(i)}=a_i. This operation permutes the coordinates; it does not merge assignments.

Theorem SNG-F03 (isomorphism invariance with original multiplicity). Graph isomorphisms preserve LGL_G, BGB_G, and ℬG\mathcal B_G.

Proof. Coordinate permutation is a bijection on profiles and on normalized profiles. It preserves the sum, minimum, and maximum of their coordinates. Since it is a bijection on edges, it preserves the sum of squared differences. Each coefficient population is therefore carried bijectively to the corresponding population for HH. ▫\square

The theorem proves one implication: isomorphic graphs have equal observations. It does not prove the converse. An invariant is allowed to identify nonisomorphic graphs. The inverse program investigates whether this particular invariant does so, and, if it does, which features remain recoverable despite that blindness.

For example, a single edge has energy (a0−a1)2(a_0-a_1)^2. A normalized nonzero profile is either (h,0)(h,0) or (0,h)(0,h), so ℬK2(x,q,z)=1+2∑h≥1xhqh2zh. \mathcal B_{K_2}(x,q,z)=1+2\sum_{h\ge1}x^h q^{h^2}z^h. The coefficient two records the two original assignments. It is not replaced by one because the edge has an endpoint-exchanging symmetry. This elementary example is a useful check on every later convention.

For a slightly richer example, take the three-vertex path 0−1−20-1-2. Its degrees are (1,2,1)(1,2,1), and direct enumeration gives [x]BG=2q+q2,[x2]BG=2q+q2+2q4+q8. [x]B_G=2q+q^2, \qquad [x^2]B_G=2q+q^2+2q^4+q^8. At volume two, placing both units at an endpoint contributes q4q^4, placing both at the middle contributes q8q^8, and placing one unit at each of two vertices contributes the remaining terms. The full mark separates the two mechanisms: [x2]ℬG=z(2q+q2)+z2(2q4+q8). [x^2]\mathcal B_G =z(2q+q^2)+z^2(2q^4+q^8). The span-one term consists of three binary subsets. The span-two term consists of three profiles concentrated at one vertex. Setting z=1z=1 adds these two populations without recording which mechanism produced each contribution.

At volume three, the unnormalized count contains the all-one profile, whose energy is zero. The normalized coefficient removes that one translation of the zero profile: [x3]BG=2q2+4q5+2q9+q18. [x^3]B_G=2q^2+4q^5+2q^9+q^{18}. Its coefficient sum is nine, compared with ten weak compositions of three into three parts. Thus normalization changes an original population by a precisely specified quotient rule; it does not arbitrarily discard an inconvenient solution. A useful calculation record should make this distinction visible whenever normalized and unnormalized outputs appear together.

For comparison, the triangle has [x]BK3=3q2,[x2]BK3=3q2+3q8. [x]B_{K_3}=3q^2, \qquad [x^2]B_{K_3}=3q^2+3q^8. Already the first coefficient distinguishes the two graphs because their degree histograms differ. Such an example checks conventions but is not a demanding test of an inverse method. Later comparisons should deliberately match the simpler observations before attributing a discrepancy to a deeper mechanism.

1.5 What a result in this book means

Several mathematical activities appear together, and their conclusions should not be conflated. A proved identity between formal series applies coefficientwise to every allowed input. An exact finite computation establishes the cells actually enumerated. A comparison through volume MM establishes equality or discrepancy through that volume. A numerical graph search may suggest a pattern without proving that no later counterexample exists. An analytic theorem requires its own convergence and continuation hypotheses even when its starting Euler factors have exact coefficients.

The book therefore separates mathematical propositions, software behavior, finite examples, and research targets. The numbered foundational statements below are proved from their displayed hypotheses. They are mathematical statements, not assertions that a proof assistant checked the implementation. Software validation supplies another kind of evidence: it tests whether a program realizes the stated mathematics on the cases examined.

Type of statement Appropriate evidence Scope of conclusion
Exact forward coefficient Enumeration, recurrence, or an exact algebraic identity The stated coefficient or family
Prefix agreement Equal coefficient dictionaries through a declared volume That finite prefix
Strict separation One exact unequal coefficient The two observations differ
Reconstruction theorem A proof recovering isomorphism from equality Every graph in the proved class
Reconstruction conjecture A precise proposed implication A question, not an established result
Analytic continuation A convergent factorization on a stated domain That domain and chosen branches

There is also a useful distinction between a new question for this project and a historically new mathematical construction. Integer graph lattices, Ising-type observations, graph partition functions, and inverse problems all have substantial literatures. The graph cut-lattice viewpoint belongs to established background, including [BHN1997]. Binary energy populations overlap directly with graph Ising polynomials with an external field; [AM2009] is relevant background. General graph reconstruction from families of observations must be compared carefully with the much richer families studied in [Lovasz2012]. No historical priority claim is needed to make the present calculations worthwhile.

The particular program here is to track exactly which relational information survives a succession of increasingly marked arithmetic height observations. Its central difficulty is lost correspondence. Counts can be exact while the identities responsible for them are absent. An inverse theorem must recover what that loss hides; an impossibility theorem must demonstrate that the lost information cannot be recovered from the declared observation. Both are substantive mathematical outcomes.

The next chapter puts the translation quotient on an integral lattice. The third chapter explains why multiple nested boundaries retain more information than a single binary cut and why repeated levels cannot be omitted. The fourth chapter turns coefficient order into a precise hierarchy of visibility, beginning with degrees and degree mixing and ending with the open reconstruction question.

2 Graphs, integral cut lattices, and the height mark

2.1 The quadratic form and its kernel

Let GG have adjacency matrix AA, degree matrix D=diag(di)D=\operatorname{diag}(d_i), and combinatorial Laplacian ΔG=D−A\Delta_G=D-A. Expanding each square in the definition of energy gives EG(a)=a⊤ΔGa=∑idiai2−2∑{i,j}∈Eaiaj. E_G(a)=a^\top\Delta_Ga =\sum_i d_i a_i^2-2\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}a_i a_j. The Laplacian is symmetric and positive semidefinite. This is stronger than a numerical spectral observation: the displayed edge-sum expression proves positivity for every real vector.

Theorem SNG-F04 (zero energy and component constants). For a∈ℝka\in\mathbb R^k, EG(a)=0E_G(a)=0 if and only if aa is constant on each connected component. In particular, for connected GG, kerΔG=ℝ𝟏\ker\Delta_G=\mathbb R\mathbf1.

Proof. A finite sum of nonnegative squares vanishes precisely when every summand vanishes. Thus adjacent vertices must have equal coordinates. Equality propagates along paths, proving constancy on every component. The converse follows because every edge lies within a component. Finally, ΔGa=0\Delta_Ga=0 implies a⊤ΔGa=0a^\top\Delta_Ga=0; component constancy also directly implies ΔGa=0\Delta_Ga=0. ▫\square

For connected graphs, the zero direction is common translation. For disconnected graphs there are additional zero directions: different components can be shifted independently. This difference matters when a formal series is evaluated without its height mark. Quotienting only by global translation does not remove all zero modes of a disconnected graph.

2.2 An orientation is a bookkeeping choice

Choose an arbitrary orientation of every edge. Let ∂\partial be the |E||E|-by-kk matrix whose row for an oriented edge i→ji\to j has −1-1 in column ii, +1+1 in column jj, and zero elsewhere. Then (∂a)i→j=aj−ai,∂⊤∂=ΔG. (\partial a)_{i\to j}=a_j-a_i, \qquad \partial^\top\partial=\Delta_G. The image 𝒞(G)=∂ℤk⊆ℤE \mathcal C(G)=\partial\mathbb Z^k\subseteq\mathbb Z^E is the integral cut, or tension, lattice in this convention. It consists of edge differences produced by integer vertex potentials. An arbitrary integer edge vector need not lie in this image: differences around every oriented cycle must sum to zero.

Reversing an edge orientation multiplies the corresponding coordinate by −1-1. This is an integral orthogonal transformation of ℤE\mathbb Z^E. It preserves inner products, squared lengths, and every energy count. An orientation is therefore needed to write vectors, but none of the observations depends on it.

Theorem SNG-F05 (integer quotient and cut-lattice coordinates). If GG is connected, a↦∂aa\mapsto\partial a induces an isomorphism of abelian groups ℤk/ℤ𝟏≅𝒞(G). \mathbb Z^k/\mathbb Z\mathbf1\ \cong\ \mathcal C(G). Under this isomorphism, squared lattice length is EG(a)E_G(a). If a root vertex rr is fixed and ΔG(r)\Delta_G^{(r)} is obtained by deleting row and column rr, the energy in rooted coordinates is the positive-definite integral form u⊤ΔG(r)u,u∈ℤk−1. u^\top\Delta_G^{(r)}u,\qquad u\in\mathbb Z^{k-1}.

Proof. The map is surjective onto its stated image. Its integer kernel consists of constant integer vectors by Theorem SNG-F04. The first isomorphism theorem gives the quotient description. The equality of squared length and energy follows from ∂⊤∂=ΔG\partial^\top\partial=\Delta_G. Every integer translation class has a unique representative with coordinate ar=0a_r=0, obtained by subtracting ar𝟏a_r\mathbf1. Substitution gives the reduced quadratic form. If that form vanishes, its full representative is constant and has root coordinate zero, so it is zero. The form is therefore positive definite. ▫\square

The root-zero representative is particularly convenient for linear algebra. It may have negative coordinates. The minimum-zero representative used by BGB_G is particularly convenient for a nonnegative height mark. These are two coordinate choices on the same quotient, not two different populations of translation classes.

2.3 A determinant that counts trees

The determinant of the reduced Laplacian gives a useful consistency check connecting the integer form with ordinary graph structure. We include a proof because it makes clear which combinatorial data enter the lattice and because no floating-point eigenvalue calculation is needed.

Theorem SNG-F06 (matrix-tree determinant). For connected GG on k≥2k\ge2 vertices and any root rr, detΔG(r)=τ(G), \det\Delta_G^{(r)}=\tau(G), where τ(G)\tau(G) is the number of spanning trees of GG.

Proof. Delete column rr of ∂\partial, obtaining MM. Then ΔG(r)=M⊤M\Delta_G^{(r)}=M^\top M. The Cauchy–Binet formula gives det(M⊤M)=∑F⊆E,|F|=k−1det(MF)2, \det(M^\top M) =\sum_{F\subseteq E,\ |F|=k-1}\det(M_F)^2, where MFM_F restricts MM to the selected edge rows. If (V,F)(V,F) is disconnected, choose a component not containing rr. Its indicator vector, restricted to nonroot coordinates, is a nonzero vector killed by MFM_F, so the determinant is zero. A connected graph with kk vertices and k−1k-1 edges is a tree. For a tree, the determinant is ±1\pm1: repeatedly choose a nonroot leaf, expand in its column, and delete the leaf and its incident edge. Each expansion contributes a sign and an entry ±1\pm1; the final empty determinant is one. Thus exactly the spanning-tree subsets contribute one to the sum. ▫\square

The theorem identifies a lattice determinant. It does not say that this determinant determines the lattice or the graph. Many nonisomorphic graphs have the same number of spanning trees. Even a complete list of real Laplacian eigenvalues describes the quadratic form only up to real orthogonal change of coordinates, whereas an integer height population depends on where the integer lattice sits inside that real space.

This distinction is elementary but decisive. A real orthogonal matrix preserves lengths of all real vectors. It need not map ℤk−1\mathbb Z^{k-1} to itself. An integral change of lattice basis must lie in GLk−1(ℤ)\mathrm{GL}_{k-1}(\mathbb Z), a much more restrictive group. Consequently equal real spectra alone do not supply a bijection between integer height profiles.

2.4 Unmarked theta and the extra information in a mark

For connected GG, the unmarked cut-lattice theta series is ΘG(q)=∑u∈ℤk−1qu⊤ΔG(r)u. \Theta_G(q)=\sum_{u\in\mathbb Z^{k-1}} q^{u^\top\Delta_G^{(r)}u}. Changing the root changes the integral coordinates but not the translation classes being counted. Likewise, an integral isometry of cut lattices preserves this series. Graph cut lattices and their relationship with graph structure have a substantial established theory; [BHN1997] provides relevant background. No converse classification from theta-series equality is assumed here.

Theorem SNG-F07 (finite energy shells and convergence). If GG is connected and k≥2k\ge2, every energy coefficient of ΘG\Theta_G is finite, and the series converges absolutely for |q|<1|q|<1. Moreover, ΘG(q)=BG(1,q) \Theta_G(q)=B_G(1,q) as a coefficientwise formal energy series and, for |q|<1|q|<1, as a convergent sum.

Proof. In root-zero coordinates, join rr to each vertex ii by a simple path of length at most k−1k-1. The telescoping sum of edge differences and Cauchy–Schwarz give ui2≤(k−1)EG(u),∑i≠rui2≤(k−1)2EG(u). u_i^2\le(k-1)E_G(u),\qquad \sum_{i\ne r}u_i^2\le(k-1)^2E_G(u). An energy shell EG(u)=eE_G(u)=e therefore lies in a finite integer box. If 0<ρ<10<\rho<1, then ρEG(u)≤ρ∥u∥22/(k−1)2, \rho^{E_G(u)} \le\rho^{\|u\|_2^2/(k-1)^2}, and the sum of the right side is a product of convergent one-dimensional Gaussian sums. The case q=0q=0 is immediate. Finally, root-zero and minimum-zero profiles each select exactly one representative of every translation class and preserve energy. Their energy sums coincide. ▫\square

For a disconnected graph with at least two nonempty components, BG(1,q)B_G(1,q) generally diverges, even for 0<q<10<q<1: set one component to height zero and another to arbitrary common height. These are distinct normalized zero-energy profiles. The true cut lattice quotients by componentwise constants, while our normalization quotients by one global constant. Those constructions must not be silently identified.

The total-height mark retains a feature that the lattice norm alone does not name. For an arbitrary integer representative aa, define μ([a])=∑iai−kminiai,η([a])=maxiai−miniai. \mu([a])=\sum_i a_i-k\min_i a_i, \qquad \eta([a])=\max_i a_i-\min_i a_i. Both are well defined on translation classes. They equal volume and span on the minimum-zero representative. The marked theta population is therefore a lattice together with extra functions on its elements. An abstract norm-preserving lattice bijection need not preserve those functions.

2.5 The height mark is an asymmetric gauge

The function μ\mu is not a linear functional on the quotient. A change in which vertex attains the minimum changes its formula. This nonlinearity is part of what the mark observes, rather than a defect in the normalization.

Theorem SNG-F08 (gauge identities and complement reciprocity). On ℤk/ℤ𝟏\mathbb Z^k/\mathbb Z\mathbf1, the functions μ\mu and η\eta satisfy μ(α+β)≤μ(α)+μ(β),μ(tα)=tμ(α)(t∈ℤ≥0), \mu(\alpha+\beta)\le\mu(\alpha)+\mu(\beta), \qquad \mu(t\alpha)=t\mu(\alpha)\quad(t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}), μ(α)+μ(−α)=kη(α). \mu(\alpha)+\mu(-\alpha)=k\eta(\alpha). For fixed span hh, put BG,h(x,q)=[zh]ℬG(x,q,z)B_{G,h}(x,q)=[z^h]\mathcal B_G(x,q,z). This is a polynomial and obeys BG,h(x,q)=xkhBG,h(x−1,q). B_{G,h}(x,q)=x^{kh}B_{G,h}(x^{-1},q).

Proof. For representatives a,ba,b, mini(ai+bi)≥miniai+minibi\min_i(a_i+b_i)\ge\min_i a_i+\min_i b_i; subtracting kk times this inequality from the coordinate sum proves subadditivity. Nonnegative integer homogeneity is immediate. Also min(−a)=−max(a)\min(-a)=-\max(a), so adding the formulas for μ([a])\mu([a]) and μ([−a])\mu([-a]) gives k(maxa−mina)k(\max a-\min a). For reciprocity, every normalized span-hh profile has coordinates in {0,…,h}\{0,\ldots,h\}, so the set is finite. The involution a↦h𝟏−aa\mapsto h\mathbf1-a preserves energy, exchanges minimum and maximum, and changes volume from mm to kh−mkh-m. Summing over the involution proves the identity. ▫\square

The reciprocity is spanwise. After setting z=1z=1, profiles with many different hh are merged, and there is no single factor xkhx^{kh} applying to their sum. This is a concrete example of a relation visible with the full mark but not immediately expressible after that mark is forgotten.

Structure retained Natural coordinate change Quantity necessarily preserved
Real quadratic space Real orthogonal isometry Real energy
Integral cut lattice Integral lattice isometry Integer energy shells
Height-marked lattice population Bijection preserving energy and μ\mu Joint volume-energy counts
Fully marked population Bijection preserving energy, μ\mu, and η\eta Joint volume-energy-span counts

These rows are preservation requirements, not a claim that every bijection in a lower row arises from graph relabeling. The inverse problem asks precisely how much of the source graph is forced by increasingly restrictive observations.

2.6 Two endpoint calculations

At q=1q=1, energy is forgotten completely. Every coordinate contributes its own geometric series, so LG(x,1)=1(1−x)k,BG(x,1)=1−xk(1−x)k. L_G(x,1)=\frac1{(1-x)^k},\qquad B_G(x,1)=\frac{1-x^k}{(1-x)^k}. No edge appears in these expressions. At q=0q=0, only zero-energy assignments remain. If the connected components have sizes k1,…,kck_1,\ldots,k_c, Theorem SNG-F04 gives LG(x,0)=∏j=1c11−xkj,BG(x,0)=(1−xk)∏j=1c11−xkj. L_G(x,0)=\prod_{j=1}^c\frac1{1-x^{k_j}}, \qquad B_G(x,0)=(1-x^k)\prod_{j=1}^c\frac1{1-x^{k_j}}. For connected graphs this reduces to LG(x,0)=1/(1−xk)L_G(x,0)=1/(1-x^k) and BG(x,0)=1B_G(x,0)=1. Thus both endpoints erase most graph structure: one ignores every edge energy, and the other retains only exact agreement within components. An inverse experiment must retain intermediate energy information rather than relying on these endpoint values alone.

2.7 Disjoint unions and recoverable component sizes

The unnormalized series factors naturally over independent components. Normalization by one global minimum does not factor in the same way, because choosing the minimum of the combined profile couples the choice of representatives in its components. This is a useful instance in which an exact quotient must be carried through an otherwise simple product rule.

Theorem SNG-F19 (component factorization and its endpoint inverse). For graphs G,HG,H on k,ℓ≥1k,\ell\ge1 vertices, LG⊔H(x,q)=LG(x,q)LH(x,q), L_{G\sqcup H}(x,q)=L_G(x,q)L_H(x,q), BG⊔H(x,q)=1−xk+ℓ(1−xk)(1−xℓ)BG(x,q)BH(x,q). B_{G\sqcup H}(x,q) =\frac{1-x^{k+\ell}}{(1-x^k)(1-x^\ell)}B_G(x,q)B_H(x,q). Moreover, the zero-energy series LG(x,0)L_G(x,0) determines the multiset of connected-component sizes.

Proof. A profile on a disjoint union is uniquely a pair of profiles on its components. Both volume and energy add, proving the first identity. Substituting LG=BG/(1−xk)L_G=B_G/(1-x^k), and the corresponding formulas for HH and the union, proves the second identity in formal series. For the final assertion, let cjc_j be the number of components of size jj. Then LG(x,0)=∏j≥1(1−xj)−cj. L_G(x,0)=\prod_{j\ge1}(1-x^j)^{-c_j}. Formal logarithms are legitimate because the constant term is one. Expanding −log(1−xj)=∑r≥1xjr/r-\log(1-x^j)=\sum_{r\ge1}x^{jr}/r, put bn=n[xn]logLG(x,0)b_n=n[x^n]\log L_G(x,0). Then bn=∑j∣njcj. b_n=\sum_{j\mid n}j c_j. Recover c1=b1c_1=b_1 and recursively cn=1n(bn−∑j∣nj<njcj). c_n=\frac1n\left(b_n-\sum_{\substack{j\mid n\\j<n}}j c_j\right). This uniquely determines every component-size multiplicity. Only finitely many are nonzero. ▫\square

The inverse statement is deliberately modest. Zero energy knows component sizes but not the edges within a component. A path and a complete graph on the same connected vertex set have identical zero-energy series. The formal logarithm extracts exactly the available component information without pretending that it contains finer internal structure.

There is a related warning about the full span mark. The span of a concatenated pair of arbitrary profiles depends on their relative vertical placement, not just on the two individual spans. Consequently one should not multiply ℬG\mathcal B_G and ℬH\mathcal B_H and declare the result to be ℬG⊔H\mathcal B_{G\sqcup H}. A correct marked factorization would need enough additional data to retain minima, maxima, and their relative shifts. The scalar unnormalized product avoids that missing correspondence because it sums actual coordinates before applying a quotient.

The cut-lattice description clarifies why integer heights are a useful meeting point. They retain the arithmetic placement of a quadratic form, while their minimum-zero representatives supply a nonlinear order mark. The next chapter expresses that order mark through nested threshold sets. This reveals precisely what lies beyond a single binary cut.

3 Nested heights and the interaction of boundaries

3.1 A height profile is a stack of threshold sets

A binary profile chooses a subset of vertices: height one on the subset and zero outside. A general integer profile chooses several nested subsets. This description is exact, but only if consecutive threshold sets are allowed to be equal. A jump of three at one vertex crosses three integer levels even if the set of vertices above those levels never changes.

For a normalized profile a≥0a\ge0 with mina=0\min a=0 and maxa=h\max a=h, define St(a)={i∈V:ai≥t},1≤t≤h. S_t(a)=\{i\in V:a_i\ge t\},\qquad 1\le t\le h. Then ⌀≠Sh⊆Sh−1⊆⋯⊆S1⊊V,a=∑t=1h𝟏St. \varnothing\ne S_h\subseteq S_{h-1}\subseteq\cdots\subseteq S_1\subsetneq V, \qquad a=\sum_{t=1}^h\mathbf1_{S_t}. The inclusions are weak. Replacing them by strict inclusions changes the population by discarding legitimate profiles.

Theorem SNG-F09 (threshold-chain bijection). Normalized profiles of span h≥1h\ge1 are in bijection with weakly nested chains of hh nonempty proper vertex subsets. The inverse map is ai=#{t:i∈St}a_i=\#\{t:i\in S_t\}, and |a|=∑t=1h|St|. |a|=\sum_{t=1}^h|S_t|.

Proof. Threshold sets of a profile have the stated nesting. Because some coordinate is zero, S1S_1 is proper; because some coordinate is hh, ShS_h is nonempty. Conversely, nesting implies that, for each vertex, membership occurs at an initial segment of the thresholds. Thus the formula for aia_i gives exactly the original membership sets when thresholds are taken again. A vertex outside S1S_1 has height zero and a vertex in ShS_h has height hh, proving normalization and span. The volume identity follows by counting all incidences (i,t)(i,t) with i∈Sti\in S_t in two orders. ▫\square

The chain is not an auxiliary encoding with multiple extensions. It is uniquely determined by the original profile, and it reconstructs that profile uniquely. Consequently a chain-based counting algorithm preserves original assignment multiplicity without an additional correction factor.

3.2 Squared differences do not add level by level

Write cG(S)=|∂S|c_G(S)=|\partial S| for the number of edges with one endpoint in SS and one outside. For disjoint vertex sets U,WU,W, write eG(U,W)e_G(U,W) for the number of edges joining them. The ordinary integer coarea identity says ∑{i,j}∈E|ai−aj|=∑t=1hcG(St). \sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}|a_i-a_j|=\sum_{t=1}^h c_G(S_t). Our energy uses squares, so this identity alone is insufficient. An edge crossing two levels contributes four, not two. Cross terms record which nested boundaries are crossed by the same edge.

Theorem SNG-F10 (nested-boundary energy formula). For the threshold chain of a normalized profile, EG(a)=∑t=1hcG(St)+2∑1≤r<t≤heG(St,V\Sr). E_G(a)=\sum_{t=1}^h c_G(S_t) +2\sum_{1\le r<t\le h}e_G(S_t,V\setminus S_r). Equivalently, EG(a)=∑r,t=1heG(Smax(r,t),V\Smin(r,t)). E_G(a)=\sum_{r,t=1}^h e_G\bigl(S_{\max(r,t)},V\setminus S_{\min(r,t)}\bigr).

Proof. Use the oriented edge-difference matrix ∂\partial from Chapter 2 and substitute a=∑t𝟏Sta=\sum_t\mathbf1_{S_t} into EG(a)=∥∂a∥22E_G(a)=\|\partial a\|_2^2. Diagonal inner products equal cG(St)c_G(S_t). If St⊆SrS_t\subseteq S_r, an edge contributes to both gradients exactly when it joins StS_t to V\SrV\setminus S_r. On such an edge the two gradient signs agree, irrespective of the chosen orientation; otherwise at least one gradient is zero. Their inner product is therefore eG(St,V\Sr)e_G(S_t,V\setminus S_r). Expanding the squared norm proves the first formula, and pairing the two orders of each off-diagonal term proves the second. ▫\square

An edgewise proof gives the same mechanism. If endpoint heights are u<vu<v, the edge crosses exactly v−uv-u thresholds. The ordered pairs of crossed thresholds number (v−u)2(v-u)^2. The double sum counts those pairs edge by edge. This argument also explains why repeated threshold sets must remain: an edge can cross several numerically different thresholds whose vertex subsets happen to coincide.

The formula concerns pairwise edge energies throughout. The cross terms are interactions between observations of nested boundaries; they do not turn the graph Hamiltonian into a new three-body or higher-body edge law. Several boundaries can jointly reveal information that isolated boundary histograms lose, even though the underlying energy remains a sum over edges.

3.3 Two examples where repetition matters

Consider the path 0−1−20-1-2. For a=(0,2,2)a=(0,2,2), the threshold chain is S1=S2={1,2}. S_1=S_2=\{1,2\}. Each set has cut size one. The sum of the two cut sizes is two, but the actual energy is (0−2)2+(2−2)2=4(0-2)^2+(2-2)^2=4. The cross term contributes the missing two, because one edge joins S2S_2 to V\S1V\setminus S_1. A strict-chain enumeration would omit this profile entirely.

For a=(0,1,3)a=(0,1,3), the same path gives S1={1,2},S2=S3={2}. S_1=\{1,2\},\qquad S_2=S_3=\{2\}. The diagonal cut sum is three. The boundaries of S1S_1 and S2S_2 lie on different edges, so their overlap term is zero; the same holds for S1,S3S_1,S_3. The repeated pair S2,S3S_2,S_3 contributes two. The total is five, agreeing with 12+221^2+2^2.

Path profile Volume Span Diagonal cut sum Cross-term contribution Energy
(0,1,1)(0,1,1) 2 1 1 0 1
(0,2,2)(0,2,2) 4 2 2 2 4
(0,1,3)(0,1,3) 4 3 3 2 5
(0,1,2)(0,1,2) 3 2 2 0 2

The last row is also useful. Distinct boundaries can have no overlap, making the squared energy equal the coarea sum. There is no universal rule replacing the cross terms by a fixed function of the individual cut sizes. Their value depends on how the boundaries sit together in the same graph.

A four-cycle makes this failure especially explicit while holding both individual sizes and individual cut counts fixed. Let the cycle be 0−1−2−3−00-1-2-3-0, and let S={0,1,2}S=\{0,1,2\}. Consider either T={0}T=\{0\} or T′={1}T'=\{1\} as the inner threshold set. Both chains have outer size three, inner size one, and cut counts two and two. However, eG(T,V\S)=1,eG(T′,V\S)=0. e_G(T,V\setminus S)=1, \qquad e_G(T',V\setminus S)=0. The two profiles are (2,1,1,0)(2,1,1,0) and (1,2,1,0)(1,2,1,0); both have volume four and span two. Their energies are respectively six and four. Thus even the ordered list of threshold sizes and cut counts does not determine the height energy. One must also retain which boundary edges are shared.

This example does not prove that two graphs with equal complete binary cut polynomials must have different height series. Both profiles occur in the same graph, and a global inverse implication could in principle use information unavailable in this two-boundary summary. What the example proves is the narrower and useful fact that the displayed chain energy cannot be computed from its separate boundary marginals alone.

3.4 An exact chain expansion of the marked series

Combining the bijection and energy formula gives ℬG(x,q,z)=1+∑h≥1zh∑⌀≠Sh⊆⋯⊆S1⊊Vx∑t|St|q∑tcG(St)+2∑r<teG(St,V\Sr). \mathcal B_G(x,q,z)=1+ \sum_{h\ge1}z^h \sum_{\varnothing\ne S_h\subseteq\cdots\subseteq S_1\subsetneq V} x^{\sum_t|S_t|} q^{\sum_t c_G(S_t)+2\sum_{r<t}e_G(S_t,V\setminus S_r)}. This is an identity of formal series. At a specified total volume mm, only chains of length at most mm can contribute, so the coefficient remains a finite sum. The expression is also a useful specification for an independent implementation: direct weak-composition enumeration and threshold-chain enumeration must return the same marked cells.

Proposition SNG-F21 (volume-pruned chain enumeration). Fix M≥0M\ge0. The following search visits every normalized profile of volume at most MM exactly once: emit the empty chain; for every nonempty proper S1⊊VS_1\subsetneq V with |S1|≤M|S_1|\le M, emit (S1)(S_1) and recursively extend a chain (S1,…,St)(S_1,\ldots,S_t) by every nonempty St+1⊆StS_{t+1}\subseteq S_t, equal sets included, with ∑r≤t+1|Sr|≤M\sum_{r\le t+1}|S_r|\le M. If each appended level is charged cG(St+1)+2∑r≤teG(St+1,V\Sr)c_G(S_{t+1})+2\sum_{r\le t}e_G(S_{t+1},V\setminus S_r), the accumulated charge is the energy of the profile, the accumulated size is its volume and the chain length is its span.

Proof. Every emitted sequence is a weakly nested chain of nonempty sets with proper first set, so SNG-F09 maps it to a normalized profile of span equal to its length and volume equal to its total size. Conversely the threshold chain of a normalized profile of volume at most MM satisfies these constraints, and each of its prefixes has total size at most MM, because sizes are positive; the search therefore reaches it through its prefixes. Distinct emitted chains differ in some level and hence give distinct profiles, since SNG-F09 is a bijection; and the search emits each chain once, because the chain determines the sequence of choices that produced it. Termination follows because each level has size at least one, so the length is at most MM. The charge identity is SNG-F10 grouped by the later index tt of each pair r<tr<t: appending St+1S_{t+1} adds its own cut and twice its overlap with every earlier level, and with no other pair. ▫\square

Repetitions are essential. Forbidding St+1=StS_{t+1}=S_t removes exactly the profiles in which some height between 00 and the span is unused, for instance (0,2,2)(0,2,2) and (0,1,3)(0,1,3) on the path. The search is implemented in src/singularity/chains.py. It shares neither its generator nor its energy evaluation with the weak-composition engine, so agreement of the two on complete marked histograms is a genuine cross-check. For every labeled simple graph on at most five vertices and every volume at most six, the two engines agree on all 142,416 marked cells and 479,963 profiles (results/chain_agreement.json). This is a finite computation on that declared population, not a proof beyond it.

The expansion shows exactly what a binary observation omits. The binary sector reports one subset at a time, through its size and cut. A chain term refers to several nested subsets in the same graph and additionally uses their boundary-overlap counts. Separate histograms of subset sizes and cuts do not retain the correspondence needed to form these overlaps.

This statement is directional. The full marked series certainly contains the binary histogram because its span-one coefficient extracts it. It does not follow that the two-variable specialization BG(x,q)=ℬG(x,q,1)B_G(x,q)=\mathcal B_G(x,q,1) permits that same extraction. After span is forgotten, a cell of given volume and energy can receive both binary and nonbinary contributions. No inversion of that mixture is proved here.

3.5 The binary sector and its reciprocity

Define the binary cut polynomial IG(x,q)=∑S⊆Vx|S|qcG(S). I_G(x,q)=\sum_{S\subseteq V}x^{|S|}q^{c_G(S)}. Its height interpretation overlaps the external-field Ising polynomial studied in [AM2009], subject to the stated normalization of the energy and spin variables. The present definition is explicit, so no external convention is needed to compute it.

Theorem SNG-F11 (binary sector extraction). For k≥2k\ge2, [z]ℬG(x,q,z)=IG(x,q)−1−xk. [z]\mathcal B_G(x,q,z)=I_G(x,q)-1-x^k. Also IG(x,q)=xkIG(x−1,q)I_G(x,q)=x^kI_G(x^{-1},q).

Proof. A minimum-zero span-one profile takes values zero and one and contains both values. It is uniquely the indicator of a nonempty proper subset. Its volume is subset size and its energy is cut size. The omitted empty and full subsets give 11 and xkx^k. Complementation preserves cut size and sends subset size to k−|S|k-|S|, proving reciprocity. ▫\square

The symmetry pairs the two sides of a cut. We count both sides as different profiles. A side of size rr and its complement of size k−rk-r appear at their respective powers of xx; when the sizes are equal they still contribute two unless other multiplicities happen to coincide.

3.6 Minimum cuts are the first positive energy shell

For a connected graph on k≥2k\ge2 vertices, define edge connectivity by λ(G)=min⌀≠S⊊VcG(S)>0. \lambda(G)=\min_{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V}c_G(S)>0. This definition suffices here; no equivalence with a disjoint-path formulation is needed.

Theorem SNG-F12 (minimum-energy shell). Every nonzero normalized profile of span hh obeys EG(a)≥λ(G)h. E_G(a)\ge\lambda(G)h. The smallest positive energy is λ(G)\lambda(G), and its full marked population is [qλ(G)]ℬG(x,q,z)=z∑⌀≠S⊊VcG(S)=λ(G)x|S|. [q^{\lambda(G)}]\mathcal B_G(x,q,z) =z\sum_{\substack{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V\\c_G(S)=\lambda(G)}}x^{|S|}.

Proof. For every nonnegative integer dd, d2≥dd^2\ge d. Hence the energy is at least the absolute-difference sum, which by coarea is ∑tcG(St)\sum_t c_G(S_t). Every threshold set is nonempty and proper, so each cut is at least λ(G)\lambda(G). This gives the bound. An indicator of a minimum cut has energy λ(G)\lambda(G), so the bound is attained. If a nonzero profile has that energy, the bound forces h=1h=1, and then its subset must be a minimum cut. ▫\square

For a path, λ=1\lambda=1, so the first positive shell consists of the two orientations of every bridge cut. For a triangle, λ=2\lambda=2, and its six nonempty proper subsets give [q2]ℬK3(x,q,z)=3z(x+x2). [q^2]\mathcal B_{K_3}(x,q,z)=3z(x+x^2). These formulas identify the very first nonconstant energy sector. They do not recover arbitrary boundary overlaps at higher energy.

3.7 Support restrictions useful for exact computation

Several finite bounds follow directly from the profile interpretation. They identify impossible marked cells before any enumeration and provide consistency checks afterward.

Theorem SNG-F13 (volume, span, and extreme energy). Let k≥2k\ge2, and let aa be a nonzero normalized profile of volume mm and span hh. Then h≤m≤(k−1)h. h\le m\le(k-1)h. If GG is connected, EG(a)≥max{λ(G)h,⌈h2diam(G)⌉}. E_G(a)\ge\max\left\{\lambda(G)h, \left\lceil\frac{h^2}{\operatorname{diam}(G)}\right\rceil\right\}. For any graph with maximum degree Δ>0\Delta>0, the largest energy among normalized volume-mm profiles is Δm2\Delta m^2, attained exactly by a=meia=m e_i at maximum-degree vertices.

Proof. Some coordinate equals hh, so the sum is at least hh. At least one coordinate is zero and every other coordinate is at most hh, giving the upper bound. The minimum-cut bound was proved above. Choose a shortest path between a minimum-height and a maximum-height vertex. If its length is ℓ\ell, telescoping and Cauchy–Schwarz give h2≤ℓ∑e on path(∂a)e2≤diam(G)EG(a)h^2\le\ell\sum_{e\text{ on path}}(\partial a)_e^2\le\operatorname{diam}(G)E_G(a). Energy is integral, giving the ceiling. Finally, the bound EG(a)≤Δ∑iai2≤Δm2E_G(a)\le\Delta\sum_i a_i^2\le\Delta m^2 was proved in Chapter 1. The profile meim e_i at a maximum-degree vertex attains it. If equality holds and Δ>0\Delta>0, then ∑iai2=m2\sum_i a_i^2=m^2. Expanding m2m^2 shows that all products aiaja_i a_j, i≠ji\ne j, vanish; exactly one coordinate is nonzero. Its degree must be Δ\Delta. ▫\square

Thus only ⌈mk−1⌉≤h≤m \left\lceil\frac{m}{k-1}\right\rceil\le h\le m can occur in a nonzero volume-mm normalized population. For fixed hh, complementation from Chapter 2 pairs volumes mm and kh−mkh-m. A computation violating either restriction has lost a normalization condition or a multiplicity.

Nested thresholds provide the human explanation for the hierarchy studied next. One occupied unit reveals a degree. Two units reveal degree mixing. Several units can occupy different heights and thereby test several linked boundaries. The information comes from their shared placement in one relation, not from replacing the original edge law with an unrelated interaction.

3.8 Primitive height scale and exact dilation

Repeated sets also encode a common integer scale. If every nonzero coordinate of a normalized profile is divisible by dd, division by dd gives another normalized profile. Volumes and spans divide by dd, while energy divides by d2d^2. This is an exact quadratic scaling law, not an approximation valid only at large height.

Call a nonzero normalized profile primitive when the greatest common divisor of its coordinates is one; zeros do not change that greatest common divisor. Let 𝒫G(x,q,z)=∑a≥0,mina=0a≠0,gcd(a0,…,ak−1)=1x|a|qEG(a)zmaxa. \mathcal P_G(x,q,z) =\sum_{\substack{a\ge0,\ \min a=0\\a\ne0,\ \gcd(a_0,\ldots,a_{k-1})=1}} x^{|a|}q^{E_G(a)}z^{\max a}. The zero profile is excluded because its common divisor is not a positive scale.

Theorem SNG-F20 (primitive-height decomposition). For every graph on k≥2k\ge2 vertices, ℬG(x,q,z)−1=∑d≥1𝒫G(xd,qd2,zd). \mathcal B_G(x,q,z)-1 =\sum_{d\ge1}\mathcal P_G(x^d,q^{d^2},z^d). If μ\mu is the arithmetic Möbius function, characterized by ∑d∣nμ(d)=1\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d)=1 for n=1n=1 and zero otherwise, then 𝒫G(x,q,z)=∑d≥1μ(d)(ℬG(xd,qd2,zd)−1). \mathcal P_G(x,q,z) =\sum_{d\ge1}\mu(d) \bigl(\mathcal B_G(x^d,q^{d^2},z^d)-1\bigr). Both identities are coefficientwise finite in every positive volume.

Proof. Every nonzero integer profile has a unique positive greatest common divisor dd, and a unique primitive quotient b=a/db=a/d. Normalization is preserved. Direct substitution gives |a|=d|b||a|=d|b|, EG(a)=d2EG(b)E_G(a)=d^2E_G(b), and maxa=dmaxb\max a=d\max b, proving the first identity. For inversion, write TdF=F(xd,qd2,zd)T_dF=F(x^d,q^{d^2},z^d); then TdTe=TdeT_dT_e=T_{de}. Substitute the first identity in the proposed inverse. The coefficient multiplying Tn𝒫GT_n\mathcal P_G is ∑d∣nμ(d)\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(d), leaving only n=1n=1. At volume m>0m>0, only d∣md\mid m can contribute, so the rearrangement is finite coefficientwise. ▫\square

For the path example (0,2,2)(0,2,2), the primitive quotient is (0,1,1)(0,1,1): volume two becomes four, energy one becomes four, and span one becomes two. This decomposition distinguishes a genuinely new shape of height profile from an integral dilation of an earlier shape. It provides another exact observation hierarchy that can be implemented independently of threshold-chain enumeration.

Primitive height here refers only to common divisibility of integer coordinates. It does not mean a primitive graph, a primitive conductor phase, or an element primitive in a different lattice. Those notions may interact in later calculations, but their definitions must not be merged because they share a word. The decomposition itself uses no connectedness assumption, so it also applies when nonconstant componentwise profiles have zero energy.

4 Visibility depth and the loss of correspondence

4.1 Increasing volume as an observation hierarchy

The coefficient CG,m(q)=[xm]LG(x,q)C_{G,m}(q)=[x^m]L_G(x,q) reports every energy attainable with exactly mm units of nonnegative integer height, together with original assignment multiplicities. Increasing mm enlarges the set of placements that can be tested. It does not simply increase numerical precision in an unchanged observation. New occupancy patterns become available: repeated occupation of one vertex, occupation of several vertices, and different heights on linked supports.

For equal-order graphs, normalization does not change the first place at which their scalar-height observations differ. If kk is fixed, multiplication by 1−xk1-x^k has constant term one. A first nonzero coefficient cannot be removed by that multiplication because no earlier nonzero coefficient exists to cancel it.

The hierarchy must be specified before it is interpreted. A volume prefix of the two-variable series is one hierarchy; a span prefix of the fully marked series is another. The binary sector is one span layer, not one volume layer: a binary subset of size ten has volume ten and span one. Conversely, a one-vertex profile of height ten has the same volume and span ten. Keeping those distinctions prevents an observation about a binary cut polynomial from being silently transferred to an unmarked height specialization.

4.2 The first coefficients can be read by hand

Write eie_i for the unit profile at vertex ii. At volume one the only profiles are eie_i, and EG(ei)=di. E_G(e_i)=d_i. At volume two the profiles are 2ei2e_i and ei+eje_i+e_j, i<ji<j. The latter subtracts two from the sum of endpoint degrees precisely when the endpoints are adjacent. This is the first layer that couples local degrees to a relation between vertices.

Theorem SNG-F14 (coefficients through volume three). For every simple graph, CG,0(q)=1,CG,1(q)=∑iqdi, C_{G,0}(q)=1, \qquad C_{G,1}(q)=\sum_iq^{d_i}, CG,2(q)=∑iq4di+∑i<jqdi+dj−2Aij, C_{G,2}(q)=\sum_iq^{4d_i} +\sum_{i<j}q^{d_i+d_j-2A_{ij}}, and CG,3(q)=∑iq9di+∑i≠jq4di+dj−4Aij+∑i<j<ℓqdi+dj+dℓ−2eG({i,j,ℓ}). \begin{aligned} C_{G,3}(q)={}&\sum_iq^{9d_i} +\sum_{i\ne j}q^{4d_i+d_j-4A_{ij}}\\ &+\sum_{i<j<\ell}q^{d_i+d_j+d_\ell-2e_G(\{i,j,\ell\})}. \end{aligned} Here eG(S)e_G(S) denotes the number of edges induced by SS. Empty index sums are zero. For normalized coefficients, [xm]BG=CG,m−CG,m−k, [x^m]B_G=C_{G,m}-C_{G,m-k}, where CG,t=0C_{G,t}=0 for t<0t<0.

Proof. Partition the weak compositions of one, two, and three by their positive parts. The possibilities are respectively 11; 22 or 1+11+1; and 33, 2+12+1, or 1+1+11+1+1. Substitute each profile in EG(a)=∑idiai2−2∑{i,j}∈Eaiaj. E_G(a)=\sum_i d_i a_i^2-2\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}a_i a_j. The pattern 2ei+ej2e_i+e_j is indexed by ordered distinct vertices because the heights distinguish the two positions. The three-unit pattern is indexed by unordered triples. These are disjoint exhaustive cases, giving the formulas without missing multiplicities. The normalized identity is coefficient extraction from Theorem SNG-F02. ▫\square

The classification can be read as a table. Write NdN_d for the number of vertices of degree dd, Pa,bϵP_{a,b}^{\epsilon} for the number of ordered pairs (i,j)(i,j), i≠ji\ne j, with di=ad_i=a, dj=bd_j=b, Aij=ϵA_{ij}=\epsilon, and Ts,tT_{s,t} for the number of unordered triples with degree sum ss spanning tt edges. These statistics are defined from degrees and adjacency alone.

A pattern lies in the normalized population exactly when its support is smaller than kk; then its span is the displayed value. For k≤3k\le3 some patterns cover every vertex and are translations instead: the profile (1,1)(1,1) on two vertices, (2,1)(2,1) and (1,2)(1,2) on two vertices, and (1,1,1)(1,1,1) on three. The normalized identity removes exactly these. The table is implemented without profile enumeration in src/singularity/lowvolume.py. tests/test_low_volume.py compares its local, normalized and marked outputs with both the weak-composition and the level-chain enumerators on all 75 labeled graphs with at most four vertices, on the fixed pairs, and on regular graphs including the cube, the Möbius ladder, the Petersen graph, K4K_4, K3,3K_{3,3}, C5C_5 and two disjoint triangles, where the closed form in terms of order, degree and triangle count (Proposition SNG-I008) is also checked.

For example, CG,1C_{G,1} determines the degree histogram exactly: its coefficient of qdq^d is the number of vertices of degree dd. It does not identify which vertex has each degree, because coordinate labels have been summed out. That missing assignment of degrees to positions is already a small instance of lost correspondence.

Normalization matters at low volume in small graphs. For k=2k=2, [x2]BG=CG,2−1[x^2]B_G=C_{G,2}-1, removing the constant profile (1,1)(1,1). For k=3k=3, the corresponding first subtraction occurs at volume three. The uniform formula is safer than assuming that normalized and unnormalized coefficients agree at every displayed low order.

4.3 What the second coefficient adds

Define the edge degree-sum polynomial JG(q)=∑{i,j}∈Eqdi+dj. J_G(q)=\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E}q^{d_i+d_j}. This is one measure of how degrees mix across edges. It is coarser than the full joint degree matrix because different degree pairs can have the same sum, but it is already more relational than the degree histogram alone.

Theorem SNG-F15 (second-layer degree mixing). For every graph, CG,2(q)=∑iq4di+∑i<jqdi+dj+(q−2−1)JG(q). C_{G,2}(q)=\sum_iq^{4d_i} +\sum_{i<j}q^{d_i+d_j} +(q^{-2}-1)J_G(q). The expression is a polynomial: every edge has di+dj≥2d_i+d_j\ge2. For graphs G,HG,H with the same degree histogram, CG,2=CH,2⇔JG=JH. C_{G,2}=C_{H,2}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad J_G=J_H.

Proof. Separate the pair sum in Theorem SNG-F14 into edges and nonedges. Start by assigning qdi+djq^{d_i+d_j} to every pair; on an edge replace it by qdi+dj−2q^{d_i+d_j-2}. The change is the displayed correction. If degree histograms agree, both of the first two sums agree, so the difference of second coefficients is (q−2−1)(JG−JH)(q^{-2}-1)(J_G-J_H). A nonzero Laurent polynomial cannot annihilate another nonzero Laurent polynomial over the integers. Thus the difference vanishes exactly when JG−JHJ_G-J_H does. ▫\square

This proposition prevents overinterpreting an attractive example. Suppose an exact comparison gives CG,2−CH,2=2q2(1−q)3(1+q). C_{G,2}-C_{H,2}=2q^2(1-q)^3(1+q). If the graphs have the same degree histogram, then JG−JH=2q4(1−q)2. J_G-J_H=2q^4(1-q)^2. The observation has detected a difference in degree mixing. That is a valid strict separation from any matched invariants, but it is not evidence that a genuinely high-order height interaction was needed. A stronger next example should first match JGJ_G, then look for a later discrepancy.

3 33, 2+12+1, 1+1+11+1+1 Ordered degree-adjacency weights and degree-decorated triple edge counts
