The final row deliberately says “aggregated.” It is not a claim that every decorated induced-subgraph count can be independently recovered from one coefficient polynomial. Different patterns can contribute the same power of qq, and their multiplicities are then added.

4.4 A precise finite-depth comparison

For graphs G,HG,H of the same order, define their scalar-height visibility depth by r(G,H)=min{m≥0:CG,m(q)≠CH,m(q)}, r(G,H)=\min\{m\ge0:C_{G,m}(q)\ne C_{H,m}(q)\}, with r=∞r=\infty when no discrepancy exists. The same definition using [xm]BG[x^m]B_G gives the same value. A depth records how much total height is required to separate the two exact observations. It is not a claim about computation time, and it is not automatically a graph-theoretic reconstruction radius.

Theorem SNG-F16 (prefix equivalence and an ultrapseudometric). For each M≥0M\ge0, agreement of CG,mC_{G,m} for all m≤Mm\le M is an equivalence relation on graphs of fixed order. Visibility depths satisfy r(G,H)≥min{r(G,K),r(K,H)}. r(G,H)\ge\min\{r(G,K),r(K,H)\}. Consequently d(G,H)=2−r(G,H)d(G,H)=2^{-r(G,H)}, with 2−∞=02^{-\infty}=0, is an ultrapseudometric. It is a metric on the quotient obtained by identifying graphs with identical full scalar-height series.

Proof. Equality of finite coefficient lists is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. If both pairs (G,K)(G,K) and (K,H)(K,H) agree below an index r0r_0, then G,HG,H agree below that index as well. This gives the displayed inequality, including infinite depths. Exponentiating reverses the inequality and gives d(G,H)≤max{d(G,K),d(K,H)}d(G,H)\le\max\{d(G,K),d(K,H)\}. Zero distance means equality of the full series, which is exactly the relation used in the stated quotient. ▫\square

Proposition SNG-F33 (finite visibility filtration). Fix a domain 𝒟\mathcal D: the symbolic coefficients in ℤ[q]\mathbb Z[q], the span-marked counts, or the values at a parameter q0q_0 that is rational or an isolated real algebraic number. For a finite family of series with common prefix through RR, let ∼v\sim_v be agreement in 𝒟\mathcal D of every coefficient at volumes 0,…,v0,\ldots,v. Then (i) each ∼v\sim_v is an equivalence relation and ∼v+1\sim_{v+1} refines ∼v\sim_v; (ii) if two series are ∼v−1\sim_{v-1}-equivalent and differ at vv, then vv is their first difference in 𝒟\mathcal D, and the signed difference at vv is a witness; (iii) symbolic equivalence implies equivalence at every parameter, and marked equivalence implies symbolic equivalence, while the converses can fail; (iv) a class that survives to RR records agreement through RR only.

Proof. (i) Agreement of finitely many values in a set with equality is an equivalence relation, and agreeing through v+1v+1 includes agreeing through vv. (ii) follows from the definition of ∼v−1\sim_{v-1}. (iii) Evaluation at q0q_0 and forgetting the span mark are functions of the finer data, so they preserve equality. The converses fail: at q=1q=1 every series on nn vertices has coefficients (m+n−1n−1)\binom{m+n-1}{n-1}, so the spectral and binary pairs merge there although they differ symbolically. (iv) The data beyond RR were not examined. ▫\square

src/singularity/visibility.py computes these partitions with deterministic class identifiers, memberships at every volume, and a signed witness for every split. For an algebraic parameter it decides equality exactly through SNG-F31’s gcd test. It refuses a bound beyond the common prefix, and a marked dictionary must be given the bound it was computed through, since it carries no length of its own. On the census of CENSUS-v1, the symbolic and marked class counts at each volume equal those of results/small_census.json. Every connected graph with at most six vertices is separated from every other by volume six (results/visibility_filtration.json). This is a finite statement about that population, not a separation bound for larger graphs.

Calling this a pseudometric is substantive caution. If nonisomorphic graphs share the entire series, their distance is zero. Proving that this cannot happen in a graph class would be a reconstruction theorem for that class. The present definitions do not assume it.

4.5 What an occupancy coefficient can depend on

A profile of volume mm has at most mm occupied vertices. Its energy depends on the induced adjacency among those vertices and on their ambient degrees. Edges from an occupied vertex to an unoccupied vertex contribute through its degree; no further structure among unoccupied vertices enters that profile’s energy.

To state this precisely, regard the induced graph G[S]G[S] as decorated by the ambient degree did_i at every vertex of SS. Two decorated induced graphs are isomorphic when a graph isomorphism also matches those degree labels. Let the decorated tt-deck record how many subsets of size tt have each such type.

Theorem SNG-F17 (decorated-deck sufficiency for a prefix). If two graphs of the same order have equal decorated tt-decks for every t≤Mt\le M, then their scalar-height coefficients agree for every m≤Mm\le M. Their fully marked coefficients agree at those volumes as well.

Proof. Fix a nonempty support SS of size t≤mt\le m. Profiles with that exact support assign positive integers bib_i to its vertices, summing to mm. Their energies are ∑i∈Sdibi2−2∑{i,j}∈E(G[S])bibj. \sum_{i\in S}d_i b_i^2 -2\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E(G[S])}b_i b_j. A degree-preserving induced-graph isomorphism gives a coordinate-permutation bijection on these positive assignments, preserving volume, energy, and span. For normalized profiles, exact supports are proper subsets; the full-support case is excluded on both graphs because their common order is the same. Summing over matching decorated support types proves equality at each m≤Mm\le M. The zero profile contributes equally. ▫\square

This is a one-way implication. The coefficient hierarchy can be coarser than the decorated decks because it aggregates different supports and positive assignments into the same energy cells. The proposition identifies a sufficient source of indistinguishability and explains the local nature of a bounded-volume experiment without asserting an unproved inversion.

It suggests several distinct research questions. Can nonisomorphic graph families have arbitrarily large finite visibility depth? Which natural graph classes admit a uniform depth bound? Can decorated-deck constructions produce exact equal-series examples, or do higher heights eventually distinguish them? These are precise targets. Finite searches can provide examples and exclusions within their declared range, but cannot settle the unrestricted questions merely by growing a table.

4.6 Why labeled probes make reconstruction easy

Consider instead the fully vertex-marked series $$ \mathscr L_G(z_0,\ldots,z_{k-1};q) =\sum_{a\ge0}\Bigl(\prod_i z_i^{a_i}\Bigr)q^{E_G(a)}. $$ The variables now identify where each unit was placed. This is a much stronger observation than scalar total height.

Theorem SNG-F18 (labeled reconstruction at degree two). The coefficients of ℒG\mathscr L_G through total zz-degree two determine the labeled adjacency matrix of GG.

Proof. The coefficient of ziz_i is the single monomial qdiq^{d_i}, recovering did_i. For distinct i,ji,j, the coefficient of zizjz_i z_j is qdi+dj−2Aijq^{d_i+d_j-2A_{ij}}. Its exponent, together with the two recovered degrees, gives Aij=di+dj−degq([zizj]ℒG)2. A_{ij}=\frac{d_i+d_j-\deg_q([z_i z_j]\mathscr L_G)}2. Every coefficient used is a single monomial with coefficient one, so its exponent is unambiguous. ▫\square

Thus a theorem saying that arbitrary vertex-marked probes determine the graph would not resolve the difficult scalar-height inverse problem. The correspondence that makes reconstruction easy has been retained explicitly. The interesting restriction is the specialization zi=xz_i=x for all ii, which merges those individually identifiable monomials into common volume cells.

This is the same reason that general graph-observation frameworks must be compared with their actual permitted test families. Results for all graph homomorphism counts, as discussed in [Lovasz2012], concern an enormously rich set of probes. One particular partition function or one particular family of height weights does not acquire the same reconstruction power by resemblance.

4.7 Marks, specializations, and the conclusions they permit

For any observation, forgetting a mark is a deterministic map on its data. Equality before forgetting implies equality afterward. A discrepancy afterward also proves a discrepancy beforehand. The reverse implications need not hold. In particular, full span-marked equality implies binary-profile equality by Theorem SNG-F11; scalar-height equality alone is not presently proved to imply it.

Numerical specialization of qq can lose information as well. The endpoints are extreme examples: at q=1q=1 every graph of the same order has the same scalar-height series, while at q=0q=0 every connected graph has BG=1B_G=1. More generally, a nonzero polynomial discrepancy can vanish at a selected algebraic value of qq. Exact polynomial comparison is stronger than comparison at one such value. If q0q_0 is transcendental, no nonzero integer polynomial vanishes there, so an exact evaluation would preserve coefficient distinctions; that logical observation does not provide an effective exact arithmetic method for an arbitrary transcendental input.

Established implication Reason Converse available here?
Graph isomorphism ⇒\Rightarrow full marked equality Coordinate-permutation bijection Not proved
Full marked equality ⇒\Rightarrow scalar-height equality Set z=1z=1 Not proved
Full marked equality ⇒\Rightarrow binary-profile equality Extract [z][z] Not proved
Connected scalar-height equality ⇒\Rightarrow unmarked theta equality Sum finite energy shells Not proved
Same decorated decks through size MM ⇒\Rightarrow height-prefix equality through volume MM Support decomposition Not proved
Exact coefficient discrepancy ⇒\Rightarrow different graph observations Definition of equality Yes, at some coefficient if the formal series differ

Finally, a later primewise Euler lift of LGL_G should be understood as an analytic reorganization. Its coefficient at a prime power recovers the corresponding local coefficient, and the local coefficients specify every Euler factor. That lift can expose useful singularities and arithmetic asymptotics, but it does not restore correspondence already discarded by the local histogram. The forward computation, the observation hierarchy, and the inverse reconstruction problem remain distinct throughout.

The resulting program is deliberately open in the right place. We can prove what the first layers observe, identify exact sources of finite-depth agreement, and formulate complete-series reconstruction as a concrete question. We can also search for persistent blindness and treat an exact counterexample as a mathematical result. What we cannot do is promote a successful prefix calculation into a conclusion about every unseen layer. The hierarchy provides the language for making the next calculation precise.

5 Prime arithmetic: assembling relational height populations

The height population becomes an arithmetic object when one integer height is assigned to every prime valuation. This step has a precise meaning. A vertex is no longer assigned one nonnegative integer; it is assigned a positive integer, whose exponent at each prime supplies a local height. The graph compares those exponents independently at each prime. Unique factorization then assembles the comparisons into an Euler product. No relation of the form nu+nv=nwn_u+n_v=n_w is imposed, and numerical closeness of two ordinary integers is not the quantity being measured. The construction records multiplicative disagreement, prime by prime.

Throughout this chapter, G=(V,E)G=(V,E) is a finite loopless simple graph with k≥2k\ge2 vertices. Connectedness is stated where needed. For a nonnegative height vector aa, write

|a|=∑v∈Vav,EG(a)=∑{u,v}∈E(au−av)2,LG(x,q)=∑a≥0x|a|qEG(a). |a|=\sum_{v\in V}a_v,\qquad E_G(a)=\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E}(a_u-a_v)^2, \qquad L_G(x,q)=\sum_{a\ge0}x^{|a|}q^{E_G(a)}.

The coefficient of every fixed power of xx is a polynomial in qq with nonnegative integer coefficients. Thus this definition is meaningful formally before convergence is discussed. For numerical analysis we take 0≤q≤10\le q\le1, use 00=10^0=1, and initially require |x|<1|x|<1. At fixed volume nn, there are exactly (n+k−1k−1)\binom{n+k-1}{k-1} labeled profiles. Consequently

|LG(x,q)|≤(1−|x|)−k(|q|≤1). |L_G(x,q)|\le(1-|x|)^{-k}\qquad(|q|\le1).

This elementary majorant will support every exchange of sums made below. The number of vertices, rather than the number of edges, controls this convenient uniform bound. Graph structure remains in the distribution of energy among profiles of the same volume.

5.1 The arithmetic weight and its exact assembly

For a positive integer tuple n=(nv)v∈Vn=(n_v)_{v\in V}, define its relational valuation energy by

ℰG(n)=∑pmprimeEG((vp(nv))v∈V). \mathcal E_G(n)=\sum_{p\ { m prime}} E_G\bigl((v_p(n_v))_{v\in V}\bigr).

Only finitely many terms are nonzero. The definition is invariant under simultaneously multiplying all coordinates by the same positive integer: this adds the same prime valuation to every local height and does not change any difference. Such multiplication does change the product ∏vnv\prod_vn_v, so energy and size remain separate statistics. Define

ZG(s,q)=∑nv≥1qℰG(n)(∏vnv)s. Z_G(s,q)=\sum_{n_v\ge1} \frac{q^{\mathcal E_G(n)}}{(\prod_vn_v)^s}.

Theorem SNG-A01 — valuation assembly. For 0≤q≤10\le q\le1 and ℜs>1\Re s>1, the preceding Dirichlet series is absolutely convergent and

ZG(s,q)=∏pLG(p−s,q). Z_G(s,q)=\prod_pL_G(p^{-s},q).

Proof. Absolute values of the summands are bounded by ∏vnv−σ\prod_vn_v^{-\sigma}, where σ=ℜs\sigma=\Re s. Their sum is ζ(σ)k<∞\zeta(\sigma)^k<\infty. Restrict first to tuples supported on a finite set of primes. Unique factorization identifies such a tuple with one height vector for each of those primes. Its denominator factors as ∏pps|a(p)|\prod_pp^{s|a(p)|}, and its weight factors as ∏pqEG(a(p))\prod_pq^{E_G(a(p))}. Multiplication of the finitely many absolutely convergent local series gives the finite Euler product. Increasing the finite prime set exhausts all tuples. Dominated convergence, or monotone convergence for real positive ss, proves the identity. The local estimate LG(p−s,q)=1+OG(p−σ)L_G(p^{-s},q)=1+O_G(p^{-\sigma}) also establishes absolute convergence directly. ▫\square

The theorem does not claim that arithmetic assembly creates extra information about the graph. The complete local series determines the Euler product. Its value is that it transfers a local relational statistic into an analytic language in which the first surviving distinction has a sharply identifiable singularity. Subsequent chapters prove that transfer rather than treating the Euler product as decoration.

Consider a single edge with heights a,ba,b. Its energy is (a−b)2(a-b)^2. At a prime dividing only one coordinate to exponent one, the local penalty is qq. A common factor at that prime contributes no penalty. A quotient with valuation difference two contributes q4q^4, not q2q^2. Thus the energy is more sensitive to repeated unequal valuation than a simple count of unmatched prime factors. The quadratic choice is part of the definition, not a claim that it is uniquely natural. Other edge costs can be studied, but their theorems require separate hypotheses.

5.2 Removing the common factor exactly

Translation invariance of energy has a local and a global consequence. Locally it removes the common minimum height. Globally it removes the greatest common divisor of all coordinates. These are the same operation viewed through prime valuations.

Theorem SNG-A02 — common-shift factorization. Put

BG(x,q)=∑a≥0minvav=0x|a|qEG(a). B_G(x,q)=\sum_{\substack{a\ge0\\\min_va_v=0}}x^{|a|}q^{E_G(a)}.

Then, as a formal power series and for |x|<1|x|<1,

LG(x,q)=BG(x,q)1−xk. L_G(x,q)=\frac{B_G(x,q)}{1-x^k}.

Equivalently, on the quotient lattice ℤk/ℤ𝟏\mathbb Z^k/\mathbb Z\mathbf1, define

ν([a])=∑vav−kminvav. \nu([a])=\sum_va_v-k\min_va_v.

This function is well defined, and

BG(x,q)=∑[a]∈ℤk/ℤ𝟏xν([a])qEG(a). B_G(x,q)=\sum_{[a]\in\mathbb Z^k/\mathbb Z\mathbf1} x^{\nu([a])}q^{E_G(a)}.

Proof. Every nonnegative profile has a unique decomposition a=b+m𝟏a=b+m\mathbf1, with m=minam=\min a and minb=0\min b=0. Its energy equals EG(b)E_G(b), and its volume is |b|+km|b|+km. Summing xkmx^{km} over m≥0m\ge0 gives the geometric factor. Every integer profile has a unique translate with minimum zero, which proves the quotient-lattice formula. ▫\square

The quotient formula explains what the volume mark retains. The quadratic form EGE_G measures distances transverse to the constant direction. The function ν\nu additionally remembers the distinguished positive cone supplied by vertex coordinates. An abstract isometry of quadratic lattices need not preserve that function. Removing common shifts does not discard the order information; it records it on a canonical representative. This distinction is central when two unmarked energy distributions agree but their volume-marked distributions differ.

Corollary SNG-A03 — primitive tuple factorization. For ℜs>1\Re s>1,

ZG(s,q)ζ(ks)=∑nv≥1gcd(nv:v∈V)=1qℰG(n)(∏vnv)s=∏pBG(p−s,q). \frac{Z_G(s,q)}{\zeta(ks)} =\sum_{\substack{n_v\ge1\\\gcd(n_v:v\in V)=1}} \frac{q^{\mathcal E_G(n)}}{(\prod_vn_v)^s} =\prod_pB_G(p^{-s},q).

Proof. Write every integer tuple uniquely as nv=dmvn_v=d\,m_v, where the coordinates of mm have common gcd one. Its energy is unchanged, and its denominator gains dksd^{ks}. Alternatively, common gcd one says that at every prime the minimum coordinate valuation is zero, exactly the defining local condition for BGB_G. Absolute convergence justifies both factorizations. ▫\square

Here “primitive” means a common gcd of one. It does not mean pairwise coprime coordinates. A tuple can share a factor between two vertices while having no factor common to every vertex. Confusing these conditions would change the local population and invalidate the shift factor.

5.3 Synchronization and independence as exact endpoints

At q=1q=1, all energy penalties disappear. At q=0q=0, only zero-energy profiles survive. For a connected graph these are precisely the constant profiles. Thus the same family interpolates between independent coordinates and complete synchronization, in an exact combinatorial sense.

Theorem SNG-A04 — endpoint identities. If GG is connected, then

qLG(x,q)BG(x,q)ZG(s,q)1(1−x)−k(1−xk)(1−x)−kζ(s)k0(1−xk)−11ζ(ks). \begin{array}{c|c|c|c} q&L_G(x,q)&B_G(x,q)&Z_G(s,q)\\\hline 1&(1-x)^{-k}&(1-x^k)(1-x)^{-k}&\zeta(s)^k\\ 0&(1-x^k)^{-1}&1&\zeta(ks). \end{array}

The Euler products converge respectively for ℜs>1\Re s>1 and ℜs>1/k\Re s>1/k. If the graph has connected component sizes k1,…,kck_1,\ldots,k_c, the synchronized endpoint is instead ∏jζ(kjs)\prod_j\zeta(k_js).

Proof. Independence gives a geometric series for each vertex. At zero energy every edge has equal endpoint heights, and therefore heights are constant on each connected component. The arithmetic tuple is correspondingly constant on each component. The indicated geometric and zeta factors follow. ▫\square

These endpoint identities require no limiting argument. A limit involving both qq and ss is a different problem because the singularity at s=1s=1 can amplify a small nonzero energy weight. Chapter 8 proves a uniform estimate that makes this distinction quantitative.

5.4 Minimum cuts are the first arithmetic correction

Assume now that the graph is connected, and let λ(G)\lambda(G) be its edge connectivity. A minimum cut is a nonempty proper vertex set whose edge boundary has size λ\lambda. We count both sides: SS and V\SV\setminus S are separate height profiles and generally have different volumes.

Theorem SNG-A05 — first positive energy. Among nonconstant integer profiles, the least energy is λ\lambda. Among minimum-zero profiles, the profiles of energy λ\lambda are exactly 𝟏S\mathbf1_S for minimum cuts SS. Consequently

[qλ]BG(x,q)=∑⌀≠S⊊V|∂S|=λx|S|,[qe]BG=0(0<e<λ). [q^\lambda]B_G(x,q)= \sum_{\substack{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V\\|\partial S|=\lambda}}x^{|S|}, \qquad [q^e]B_G=0\quad(0<e<\lambda).

Proof. For an integer difference dd, d2≥|d|d^2\ge|d|. If aa has minimum zero and span hh, then the discrete coarea identity gives

∑{u,v}|au−av|=∑t=0h−1|∂{v:av>t}|. \sum_{\{u,v\}}|a_u-a_v| =\sum_{t=0}^{h-1}|\partial\{v:a_v>t\}|.

Every level set in that sum is nonempty and proper, so EG(a)≥λhE_G(a)\ge\lambda h. A nonzero minimum-zero profile has h≥1h\ge1. A binary minimum-cut profile attains energy λ\lambda. If energy equals λ\lambda, the bound forces h=1h=1, and the profile is the indicator of a minimum cut. ▫\square

Write P(z)=∑pp−zP(z)=\sum_pp^{-z} for the prime zeta function on its initial half-plane. The first positive energy coefficient now has an exact analytic description.

Theorem SNG-A06 — minimum-cut prime-zeta coefficient. Initially for ℜs>1\Re s>1,

[qλ]logZG(s,q)ζ(ks)=∑⌀≠S⊊V|∂S|=λP(|S|s). [q^\lambda]\log\frac{Z_G(s,q)}{\zeta(ks)} =\sum_{\substack{\varnothing\ne S\subsetneq V\\|\partial S|=\lambda}} P(|S|s).

Proof. The constant coefficient in qq of BGB_G is one, and there are no positive coefficients below degree λ\lambda. Hence its first positive coefficient is unchanged by the formal logarithm. Apply Theorem SNG-A05 to logBG(p−s,q)\log B_G(p^{-s},q), and sum over primes. Absolute convergence on ℜs>1\Re s>1, uniformly for qq in a sufficiently small complex disk, justifies coefficient extraction. This uniformity also follows from the local majorant and the fact that each normalized factor equals one at q=0q=0. ▫\square

A cut with a large side contributes at a different scaled argument than a cut with a small side. The coefficient therefore contains the sizes of oriented minimum-cut sides, not merely their number. It also identifies the scope of this first correction: it sees minimum cuts only. Higher energy coefficients mix larger cuts with profiles having several height levels. Extracting those sectors requires retained marks or additional identities; the first coefficient alone does not reconstruct the graph.

5.5 Two small models that expose the retained information

For the graph consisting of a single edge, a minimum-zero profile is either (0,0)(0,0), (h,0)(h,0), or (0,h)(0,h), with h≥1h\ge1. Thus there is a closed local formula

BK2(x,q)=1+2∑h≥1qh2xh,LK2(x,q)=1+2∑h≥1qh2xh1−x2. B_{K_2}(x,q)=1+2\sum_{h\ge1}q^{h^2}x^h, \qquad L_{K_2}(x,q)=\frac{1+2\sum_{h\ge1}q^{h^2}x^h}{1-x^2}. \tag{5.1}

The exponent h2h^2 records a genuinely unequal-height sector. Replacing it by hh would give a different model even though the first positive-energy coefficient would agree. The first minimum-cut correction is 2P(s)2P(s): either coordinate can be the raised endpoint. At volume two the three original profiles are (2,0),(1,1),(0,2)(2,0),(1,1),(0,2), with energy histogram 1+2q41+2q^4. Normalization removes the common-shift profile (1,1)(1,1), leaving 2q42q^4. This small calculation separates labeled population counting, common-factor removal, and energy weighting without relying on a large graph example.

For the path on three vertices, choose its middle vertex as a root and write the edge differences as u=a1−a0u=a_1-a_0 and v=a2−a0v=a_2-a_0. There is one integer profile modulo common translation for every pair (u,v)∈ℤ2(u,v)\in\mathbb Z^2. Its minimum-zero volume is

ν=u+v−3min(0,u,v),E=u2+v2. \nu=u+v-3\min(0,u,v), \qquad E=u^2+v^2.

Consequently

BP3(x,q)=∑u,v∈ℤqu2+v2xu+v−3min(0,u,v). B_{P_3}(x,q)=\sum_{u,v\in\mathbb Z} q^{u^2+v^2}x^{u+v-3\min(0,u,v)}. \tag{5.2}

The energy has independent coordinates, but the volume does not. The minimum couples them through which vertex is lowest. This is a direct elementary instance of metric information being simpler than order information. It also illustrates why a factorization of an unmarked theta series does not automatically factor its volume-marked refinement.

Theorem SNG-A19 — all trees share the unmarked energy theta. Let TT be any tree with kk vertices, and let

ϑ(q)=∑h∈ℤqh2. \vartheta(q)=\sum_{h\in\mathbb Z}q^{h^2}.

For 0≤q<10\le q<1,

BT(1,q)=ϑ(q)k−1. B_T(1,q)=\vartheta(q)^{k-1}. \tag{5.3}

Proof. Choose a root and orient every edge away from it. Sending a vertex profile modulo common integer translation to its k−1k-1 oriented edge differences is a bijection with ℤk−1\mathbb Z^{k-1}. Injectivity follows by propagating equal differences along the unique root-to-vertex paths. Surjectivity follows by starting the root at zero and integrating the prescribed integer differences along those paths. Energy becomes the sum of squares of the independent edge differences. At x=1x=1, the minimum-zero representative introduces no extra weight, so the sum factors into k−1k-1 copies of ϑ\vartheta. Absolute convergence follows from the convergent one-dimensional Gaussian series. ▫\square

This is a useful family of exact collisions, not merely a single searched pair. Every tree of a fixed order has the same unmarked energy distribution. The marked series can already distinguish a four-vertex path from a four-vertex star at volume one: the first has degree polynomial 2q+2q22q+2q^2, the second 3q+q33q+q^3. Their unmarked quadratic lattices agree, yet the coordinate cone places the lattice vectors into different volume layers. More demanding matched examples must remove this elementary degree explanation, but the family makes the logical source of the restored information unmistakable.

Connectedness matters to an unmarked specialization. If the graph has several components, removing one global common shift leaves independent relative component shifts of zero energy. The sum BG(1,q)B_G(1,q) then diverges, even when q<1q<1. The local series at |x|<1|x|<1 remains perfectly well defined. On disconnected graphs it is preferable to normalize one common shift per component before setting the volume variable to one. Ordinary component factorization gives

LG(x,q)=∏j=1cLGj(x,q), L_G(x,q)=\prod_{j=1}^cL_{G_j}(x,q),

while the single-shift normalized series is

BG(x,q)=1−xk∏j(1−xkj)∏jBGj(x,q). B_G(x,q)= \frac{1-x^k}{\prod_j(1-x^{k_j})}\prod_jB_{G_j}(x,q).

The remaining denominator is the exact record of those unconstrained relative shifts. This is an example where checking the meaning of a normalization prevents a misleading finite theta interpretation.

6 Euler analysis: formal coordinates and controlled analytic factors

An Euler product has two distinct kinds of structure in this project. Its coefficients are exact finite polynomials, so logarithms and Euler transforms can be manipulated formally. Its values are infinite products, so analytic conclusions additionally require convergence and choices of branches. The distinction is useful rather than restrictive. Formal calculations reveal which factor ought to be removed; a remainder estimate proves where that removal has analytic meaning. The results below keep those two steps explicit.

Fix a graph with kk vertices, write

L(x,q)=1+∑n≥1ℓn(q)xn,ℓn(q)=∑|a|=nqE(a), L(x,q)=1+\sum_{n\ge1}\ell_n(q)x^n, \qquad \ell_n(q)=\sum_{|a|=n}q^{E(a)},

and initially regard qq as an indeterminate. Every ℓn\ell_n belongs to ℤ≥0[q]\mathbb Z_{\ge0}[q]. Formal logarithms belong to ℚ[q][[x]]\mathbb Q[q][[x]], because division by positive integers enters the logarithm expansion. No numerical approximation to qq, the coefficients, or the graph enters this part of the theory.

6.1 Logarithmic coordinates from finite data

Put logL=∑n≥1cn(q)xn\log L=\sum_{n\ge1}c_n(q)x^n. The identity L′=L(logL)′L'=L(\log L)' gives a triangular recurrence that computes each logarithmic coefficient using only the local coefficients through the same volume:

cn=ℓn−1n∑j=1n−1jcjℓn−j. c_n=\ell_n-\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}j\,c_j\ell_{n-j}. \tag{6.1}

In particular,

c1=ℓ1,c2=ℓ2−ℓ12/2,c3=ℓ3−ℓ1ℓ2+ℓ13/3. c_1=\ell_1,\quad c_2=\ell_2-\ell_1^2/2,\quad c_3=\ell_3-\ell_1\ell_2+\ell_1^3/3.

The recurrence is a coefficient identity, not a fitted model. If two graphs agree through volume r−1r-1, they also agree in logarithmic coordinates through that volume, and their difference at volume rr is unchanged. This triangular property is the reason first-discrepancy singularities can be read directly from the original local coefficients.

Theorem SNG-A07 — rational polynomial Euler transform. There is a unique sequence bm(q)∈ℚ[q]b_m(q)\in\mathbb Q[q] such that, formally in xx,

L(x,q)=∏m≥1(1−xm)−bm(q). L(x,q)=\prod_{m\ge1}(1-x^m)^{-b_m(q)}. \tag{6.2}

It is given by

bm(q)=∑d∣mμ(d)dcm/d(q). b_m(q)=\sum_{d\mid m}\frac{\mu(d)}d\,c_{m/d}(q). \tag{6.3}

Only factors with m≤Nm\le N affect coefficients through volume NN.

Proof. Taking formal logarithms of the proposed product gives

cn=1n∑m∣nmbm. c_n=\frac1n\sum_{m\mid n}m b_m.

Ordinary Möbius inversion gives (6.3). Conversely those coefficients satisfy the displayed logarithmic identity, and formal exponential recovers LL. Uniqueness follows from the same triangular relation. Rational polynomial exponents are meaningful through the formal exponential definition of (1−xm)−bm(1-x^m)^{-b_m}. ▫\square

The first exponents are

b1=ℓ1,b2=ℓ2−ℓ12+ℓ12, b_1=\ell_1,\qquad b_2=\ell_2-\frac{\ell_1^2+\ell_1}{2},

b3=ℓ3−ℓ1ℓ2+ℓ13−ℓ13. b_3=\ell_3-\ell_1\ell_2+\frac{\ell_1^3-\ell_1}{3}.

The implementation follows these identities literally and keeps them independent. series_log uses the recurrence (6.1); euler_exponents solves ncn=∑d∣ndbdnc_n=\sum_{d\mid n}db_d upward; euler_exponents_mobius applies (6.3); and recompose_euler rebuilds LL by multiplying the generalized binomial series (1−xm)−bm=∑j(bm+j−1j)xmj(1-x^m)^{-b_m}=\sum_j\binom{b_m+j-1}{j}x^{mj}, without any logarithm. All arithmetic is in ℚ[q]\mathbb Q[q] with reduced fractions, and a prefix through volume NN determines exactly the exponents b1,…,bNb_1,\ldots,b_N. Tests check the triangular identity on a seven-vertex graph series, the single-edge values (6.10), recomposition of every retained certificate’s exponents, nonconstant rational exponents and a symbolic discrepancy that vanishes at q=1q=1, so that the specialized first difference moves to a later volume.

These formulas are economical coordinates for local information. They do not make every exponent nonnegative or integral as a polynomial in qq. Such claims would be false for general integer-coefficient series. The existence theorem is over ℚ[q]\mathbb Q[q], where the necessary divisions are legitimate.

Common-shift removal has an especially simple Euler-coordinate description. If B=(1−xk)LB=(1-x^k)L, then

bm(L)=bm(B)+𝟏m=k. b_m(L)=b_m(B)+\mathbf1_{m=k}.

At the connected synchronized endpoint the only nonzero exponent is bk=1b_k=1. At the independent endpoint the only nonzero exponent is b1=kb_1=k. These are useful exact consistency checks, but they do not determine intermediate exponents from the endpoints.

6.2 A different transform keeps integral bidegrees

There is a second, genuinely different product decomposition. Instead of putting a polynomial exponent on 1−xm1-x^m, retain energy inside the individual factors:

L(x,q)=∏m≥1∏e≥0(1−xmqe)−Nm,e. L(x,q)=\prod_{m\ge1}\prod_{e\ge0} (1-x^m q^e)^{-N_{m,e}}. \tag{6.4}

At each fixed mm, only finitely many Nm,eN_{m,e} are nonzero. The exponents can be negative. This is a formal decomposition and does not identify an actual population of positive “atoms” without a separate positivity theorem.

Theorem SNG-A08 — integral bidegree transform. For every series L∈1+xℤ[q][[x]]L\in1+x\mathbb Z[q][[x]], there are unique integers Nm,eN_{m,e} satisfying (6.4). Their generating series is the plethystic logarithm

∑m,eNm,exmqe=∑d≥1μ(d)dlogL(xd,qd). \sum_{m,e}N_{m,e}x^m q^e =\sum_{d\ge1}\frac{\mu(d)}d\log L(x^d,q^d). \tag{6.5}

Proof. Suppose all factors of volume below mm have been removed. The remaining series has the form 1+xmPm(q)+O(xm+1)1+x^mP_m(q)+O(x^{m+1}), with integral polynomial PmP_m. For every coefficient Nm,e=[qe]PmN_{m,e}=[q^e]P_m, multiply by (1−xmqe)Nm,e(1-x^mq^e)^{N_{m,e}}. This removes volume mm and preserves integrality. Induction gives existence and uniqueness. Taking logarithms of (6.4), and applying Möbius inversion to the simultaneous substitutions (x,q)↦(xd,qd)(x,q)\mapsto(x^d,q^d), gives (6.5). Thus the apparently rational expression in (6.5) has integral coefficients. ▫\square

The substitution q↦qdq\mapsto q^d is essential. Omitting it computes the transform in Theorem SNG-A07 rather than the bidegree transform. The two descriptions organize the same formal series differently. For example, a factor (1−xq)−1(1-xq)^{-1} has one bidegree atom, yet its ordinary exponents bm(q)b_m(q) are generally nontrivial polynomials. Coefficient-level equality permits conversion; the interpretations should remain distinct.

The corresponding weighted arithmetic factor is

𝒵m,e(s,q)=∏p(1−qep−ms)−1, \mathcal Z_{m,e}(s,q)=\prod_p(1-q^ep^{-ms})^{-1},

with logarithm, on its absolutely convergent domain,

log𝒵m,e(s,q)=∑j≥1qejjP(mjs). \log\mathcal Z_{m,e}(s,q) =\sum_{j\ge1}\frac{q^{ej}}jP(mjs).

It is not equal to ζ(ms)qe\zeta(ms)^{q^e}. Replacing one expression by the other discards all the terms involving qejq^{ej} for j>1j>1. The ordinary rational-exponent transform and the integral bidegree transform therefore lead to different useful analytic factorizations.

6.3 Leading divergence and what it forgets

The first local coefficient has a simple graph formula:

αG(q)=ℓ1(q)=∑v∈Vqdv. \alpha_G(q)=\ell_1(q)=\sum_{v\in V}q^{d_v}.

Only one vertex has height one in a volume-one profile. Its energy is the number of incident edges. Thus the dominant singularity records the degree multiset and no finer graph information.

Theorem SNG-A09 — leading real singularity. For fixed 0≤q≤10\le q\le1, define

HG(s,q)=∏p(1−p−s)αG(q)LG(p−s,q). H_G(s,q)=\prod_p(1-p^{-s})^{\alpha_G(q)}L_G(p^{-s},q). \tag{6.6}

The product is holomorphic for ℜs>1/2\Re s>1/2, using the analytic logarithm of 1−p−s1-p^{-s} defined by its convergent power series on ℜs>0\Re s>0. It is positive at the real point s=1s=1 and holomorphic and nonzero in a complex neighborhood of that point. Initially for ℜs>1\Re s>1,

ZG(s,q)=ζ(s)αG(q)HG(s,q). Z_G(s,q)=\zeta(s)^{\alpha_G(q)}H_G(s,q).

Along the positive real axis,

ZG(1+ε,q)∼HG(1,q)ε−αG(q)(ε↓0). Z_G(1+\varepsilon,q) \sim H_G(1,q)\varepsilon^{-\alpha_G(q)} \qquad(\varepsilon\downarrow0). \tag{6.7}

Proof. Locally L=1+αx+O(x2)L=1+\alpha x+O(x^2), uniformly for q∈[0,1]q\in[0,1]. Multiplication by (1−x)α(1-x)^\alpha cancels the linear coefficient, leaving 1+O(x2)1+O(x^2). The prime sum of the remainder converges normally on compact subsets of ℜs>1/2\Re s>1/2. Each individual factor is holomorphic there; LL is analytic on |x|<1|x|<1, and the chosen power is holomorphic on ℜs>0\Re s>0. For real positive ss, all factors are positive. The infinite tail is nonzero by absolute convergence of its logarithm; finitely many remaining factors are nonzero in a neighborhood of s=1s=1. The factorization follows on the original domain from the usual zeta Euler product. Finally ζ(1+ε)∼1/ε\zeta(1+\varepsilon)\sim1/\varepsilon. ▫\square

The word “holomorphic” in the theorem does not assert that HGH_G is zero-free throughout its half-plane. A finite local factor can have complex zeros. Nonvanishing is asserted near the positive real point where it is proved. Similarly, fractional powers of zeta are unambiguous on the original half-plane but need branch choices if continued around zeros or poles elsewhere.

6.4 Finite-order zeta factorization

Theorem SNG-A10 — controlled finite Euler extraction. Fix an integer M≥1M\ge1 and a numerical q∈[0,1]q\in[0,1]. Put

HG,M(s,q)=∏pLG(p−s,q)∏m=1M(1−p−ms)bm(q). H_{G,M}(s,q)=\prod_p L_G(p^{-s},q) \prod_{m=1}^{M}(1-p^{-ms})^{b_m(q)}. \tag{6.8}

This product is holomorphic on ℜs>1/(M+1)\Re s>1/(M+1). It is positive for real s>1/(M+1)s>1/(M+1), and nonzero in a neighborhood of every point on that positive real interval. On the initial half-plane,

ZG(s,q)=(∏m=1Mζ(ms)bm(q))HG,M(s,q). Z_G(s,q)= \left(\prod_{m=1}^{M}\zeta(ms)^{b_m(q)}\right)H_{G,M}(s,q). \tag{6.9}

Proof. Theorem SNG-A07 implies

LG(x,q)∏m=1M(1−xm)bm(q)=1+O(xM+1) L_G(x,q)\prod_{m=1}^M(1-x^m)^{b_m(q)}=1+O(x^{M+1})

near zero. For primes sufficiently large, this estimate is uniform on any compact subset of the indicated half-plane, and its prime sum converges. The finitely many small-prime factors are holomorphic on ℜs>0\Re s>0; the powers use the logarithms specified above. Positivity on the real axis follows directly from (6.8), and absolute logarithmic convergence proves local nonvanishing there. Equation (6.9) follows by finite multiplication of zeta Euler products on ℜs>1\Re s>1. ▫\square

This theorem removes any need to assume convergence of the infinite product over all mm in an analytic setting. Formal identity (6.2) does not by itself license an unrestricted exchange of its two infinite products, over primes and over volumes. Small-prime local zeros can limit the radius of the logarithmic power series, and the exponents can grow. Keeping MM finite is both sufficient for a prescribed visibility calculation and analytically safer.

Equation (6.9) supplies local continuations after branches have been chosen in regions avoiding relevant zeta zeros and poles. It is not a blanket meromorphic-continuation theorem. Nonintegral exponents generally produce branched functions. Even on the positive real axis below one, separate zeta factors can be negative, so assigning real fractional powers independently does not reproduce an automatically positive partition function. The positive quantity directly defined there is the remainder product (6.8); its relation to a continued ZGZ_G must respect the chosen branches.

6.5 Why ratios are cleaner than individual continuations

If two graphs have identical low-volume coefficients, their low-order zeta exponents cancel before any continuation is attempted. The quotient Euler product can consequently converge farther left as a positive real product. Its first remaining zeta factor has argument approaching one from above. No lower-argument zeta powers are needed to state the resulting real asymptotic. This is the analytic advantage of comparing matched structures rather than interpreting every formal singularity of an individual object as an independently observable feature.

The hierarchy is exact but limited. It proves where a known local distinction appears arithmetically. It does not prove that a distinction always exists between nonisomorphic graphs, nor that all formal exponent locations are actual singularities after every cancellation. If the local series agree, every arithmetic lift in this chapter agrees. If the first discrepancy vanishes at a special numerical qq, the visibility order at that parameter must be recomputed. These qualifications identify the genuine inverse problem rather than weakening a theorem that never claimed more.

6.6 A complete low-order transform example

The single-edge model makes the difference between polynomial exponents and positive constituent populations concrete. Its first coefficients are

ℓ1=2q,ℓ2=1+2q4,ℓ3=2q+2q9. \ell_1=2q,\qquad \ell_2=1+2q^4,\qquad \ell_3=2q+2q^9.

Substitution into the rational Euler transform gives

b1(q)=2q,b2(q)=1+2q4−2q2−q,b3(q)=2q9−4q5+(8q3−2q)/3. \begin{aligned} b_1(q)&=2q,\\ b_2(q)&=1+2q^4-2q^2-q,\\ b_3(q)&=2q^9-4q^5+(8q^3-2q)/3. \end{aligned} \tag{6.10}

At q=1/2q=1/2, these are 1,1/8,−31/2561,1/8,-31/256. Thus a valid finite extraction reads

ZK2(s,1/2)=ζ(s)ζ(2s)1/8ζ(3s)−31/256HK2,3(s,1/2)(ℜs>1). Z_{K_2}(s,1/2)= \zeta(s)\zeta(2s)^{1/8}\zeta(3s)^{-31/256} H_{K_2,3}(s,1/2) \qquad(\Re s>1). \tag{6.11}

The negative third exponent is not a negative number of arithmetic objects. It is a subtraction introduced by logarithmic and Möbius coordinates. Likewise, the exponent one eighth does not describe one eighth of an independent integer coordinate. Those are exact algebraic coordinates on a positive local series. They are useful precisely because they can cancel lower-order contributions, not because each factor has a separate population interpretation.

At the endpoints the same formulas reduce correctly: at q=0q=0, the second exponent is one and the other displayed exponents are zero; at q=1q=1, the first exponent is two and the next two are zero. Agreement at both endpoints therefore places only weak restrictions on the intermediate polynomial behavior. The coefficient recurrence supplies the actual intermediate values. A numerical plot interpolating only the endpoints would have no authority to invent them.

The bidegree decomposition has a different bookkeeping purpose. Its first volume layer contains the atom count N1,1=2N_{1,1}=2. Removing (1−xq)−2(1-xq)^{-2} from the single-edge series leaves, at volume two, the polynomial 1−3q2+2q41-3q^2+2q^4. Hence the second bidegree layer already contains a negative exponent, N2,2=−3N_{2,2}=-3. Even integral bidegree exponents are therefore not automatically positive atoms. The notation “plethystic” supplies a formal inversion rule; it does not establish a free-generation theorem for an underlying combinatorial class.

6.7 Uniformity and the boundary of the weight parameter

For each fixed extraction order MM, the remainder product in Theorem SNG-A10 is jointly continuous in real q∈[0,1]q\in[0,1] and real s>1/(M+1)s>1/(M+1). On compact subsets of that parameter region its large-prime logarithmic tail converges uniformly. To see this, the finitely many polynomials bm(q)b_m(q) are bounded on the compact weight interval, and the coefficient majorant bounds the Taylor remainders uniformly for xx in a small fixed disk. The canceled coefficients through order MM are identically zero as polynomials, so the remaining estimate is uniformly O(xM+1)O(x^{M+1}). A convergent prime-power sum dominates the tail. Finitely many positive real local factors then preserve continuity and local nonvanishing.

This continuity statement is often enough to pass a weight limit through a regularized product. It does not mean that the unregularized Euler product converges uniformly as s↓1s\downarrow1. The leading zeta factor carries the obstruction to that stronger statement. Chapter 8 isolates it in a quantitative estimate rather than suppressing it through a formal exchange of limits.

The chosen weight range also has a mathematical boundary. Suppose the graph has an edge, choose a vertex of positive degree dvd_v, and fix 0<x<10<x<1. The terms coming from profiles nevne_v are qdvn2xnq^{d_vn^2}x^n. For every real q>1q>1, these terms fail even to tend to zero as n→∞n\to\infty. Thus the unbounded local height series diverges. The restriction q≤1q\le1 cannot simply be removed by calling the series a partition function. A finite height cutoff would define a different object and would require its own limiting argument.

For |q|<1|q|<1, the local series is analytic in the complex weight parameter. At a boundary value such as q=1q=1, derivatives from the allowed real side can still exist to every finite order, because each derivative introduces only polynomial energy factors and the geometric volume decay dominates them. Such smooth one-sided behavior should not be mistaken for an unrestricted analytic extension beyond the unit disk. These domain distinctions matter especially when symbolic exponents are evaluated numerically: exact polynomial coefficients can be evaluated anywhere, while the infinite series from which they were extracted has the domain proved for it.

7 Visibility singularities: the first distinction survives arithmetic assembly

A comparison is strongest when simpler explanations have been removed explicitly. Two graphs can have the same degree multiset and therefore the same leading divergence. They can agree on additional finite invariants and still differ in a later local height coefficient. The arithmetic question is then not whether an Euler product can be attached to each graph: that is already automatic. The useful question is where the first unmatched local observation becomes analytically visible.

For 0≤q≤10\le q\le1, put ℓG,n(q)=[xn]LG(x,q)\ell_{G,n}(q)=[x^n]L_G(x,q). In this chapter, qq is fixed before an analytic comparison is made. Polynomial equality in qq is stronger than numerical equality at a selected parameter. A polynomial discrepancy can vanish at an endpoint or an interior root, in which case the first visible volume at that numerical parameter can change.

7.1 A precise first-discrepancy theorem

Theorem SNG-A11 — first-discrepancy ratio law. Let G,HG,H have the same finite number kk of vertices. Fix q∈[0,1]q\in[0,1]. Suppose

ℓG,n(q)=ℓH,n(q)(0≤n<r),δ=ℓG,r(q)−ℓH,r(q)≠0. \ell_{G,n}(q)=\ell_{H,n}(q)\quad(0\le n<r), \qquad \delta=\ell_{G,r}(q)-\ell_{H,r}(q)\ne0. \tag{7.1}

For real s>1/rs>1/r, the ratio product

RG,H(s,q)=∏pLG(p−s,q)LH(p−s,q) R_{G,H}(s,q)=\prod_p \frac{L_G(p^{-s},q)}{L_H(p^{-s},q)} \tag{7.2}

converges absolutely to a positive number. It agrees with ZG/ZHZ_G/Z_H on the original domain s>1s>1. Define

KG,H(s,q)=∏p(1−p−rs)δLG(p−s,q)LH(p−s,q). K_{G,H}(s,q)=\prod_p (1-p^{-rs})^\delta \frac{L_G(p^{-s},q)}{L_H(p^{-s},q)}. \tag{7.3}

The latter product converges absolutely and is positive for real s>1/(r+1)s>1/(r+1). It is holomorphic and nonzero in a complex neighborhood of s0=1/rs_0=1/r. For real s>s0s>s_0,

RG,H(s,q)=ζ(rs)δKG,H(s,q),RG,H(s,q)∼C(q)(rs−1)−δ, R_{G,H}(s,q)=\zeta(rs)^\delta K_{G,H}(s,q), \qquad R_{G,H}(s,q)\sim C(q)(rs-1)^{-\delta}, \tag{7.4}

where C(q)=KG,H(1/r,q)>0C(q)=K_{G,H}(1/r,q)>0.

Proof. Condition (7.1) gives

LG(x,q)LH(x,q)=1+δxr+O(xr+1) \frac{L_G(x,q)}{L_H(x,q)} =1+\delta x^r+O(x^{r+1})

near zero, because the denominator has constant term one. The prime sum of the deviation converges for rs>1rs>1. No local denominator vanishes on the positive real axis: both local series have nonnegative coefficients and constant term one. Thus the product is positive, and its logarithm converges absolutely. Multiplication by (1−xr)δ(1-x^r)^\delta cancels the first discrepancy, leaving 1+O(xr+1)1+O(x^{r+1}). This proves convergence of (7.3) on the stated real interval.

To obtain a complex neighborhood, separate finitely many small primes from the normally convergent tail. Every small-prime denominator is positive at s0s_0, hence nonzero in a sufficiently small disk about that point. The tail is analytic and nonzero there by its convergent logarithm. The factors (1−p−rs)δ(1-p^{-rs})^\delta use the analytic logarithm defined on ℜs>0\Re s>0. This gives the asserted local holomorphic nonzero function. On s>1/rs>1/r, the ordinary zeta Euler product yields the factorization. Finally ζ(1+t)∼1/t\zeta(1+t)\sim1/t with t=rs−1t=rs-1. ▫\square

A positive discrepancy makes the ratio diverge at its visibility point; a negative discrepancy makes it tend to zero. Interchanging the graphs reverses that interpretation. If δ\delta is nonintegral, the complex singularity is a fractional-power branch singularity. It should not be called a pole. The theorem supplies a local branch and a positive-real asymptotic, not a globally single-valued meromorphic function.

There is also no requirement that the original partition functions converge separately at s0s_0. Their common low-order divergences have been canceled in the ratio product before the limit is taken. This cancellation is the main analytic mechanism. It makes a comparison meaningful farther left without pretending that either original positive Dirichlet series has acquired an absolutely convergent definition there.

7.2 A volume-two calculation and its actual meaning

At volume two there are only two kinds of profile: 2ev2e_v, and eu+eve_u+e_v with u<vu<v. Their energies give the identity

ℓG,2(q)=∑vq4dv+∑u<vqdu+dv−2Auv. \ell_{G,2}(q)=\sum_vq^{4d_v} +\sum_{u<v}q^{d_u+d_v-2A_{uv}}. \tag{7.5}

For graphs with the same degree multiset, define the edge degree-sum polynomial

MG(q)=∑{u,v}∈Eqdu+dv. M_G(q)=\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E}q^{d_u+d_v}.

Then

ℓG,2−ℓH,2=(q−2−1)(MG−MH). \ell_{G,2}-\ell_{H,2} =(q^{-2}-1)(M_G-M_H). \tag{7.6}

Although written with q−2q^{-2}, the right side is a polynomial: every edge has degree sum at least two. Formula (7.6) follows by starting with the sum over all unordered vertex pairs and correcting the exponent by minus two precisely on edges.

Calculation SNG-A12 — first reference pair. On vertices 0,…,60,\ldots,6, take

E(G)={01,02,03,04,12,35,36},E(H)={01,02,03,04,15,16,56}. \begin{aligned} E(G)&=\{01,02,03,04,12,35,36\},\\ E(H)&=\{01,02,03,04,15,16,56\}. \end{aligned}

Both have degree multiset {4,3,2,2,1,1,1}\{4,3,2,2,1,1,1\}. Exact profile enumeration gives equality at volume one and

δ2(q)=ℓG,2−ℓH,2=2q2−4q3+4q5−2q6=2q2(1−q)3(1+q). \delta_2(q)=\ell_{G,2}-\ell_{H,2} =2q^2-4q^3+4q^5-2q^6 =2q^2(1-q)^3(1+q). \tag{7.7}

It is positive on 0<q<10<q<1, so Theorem SNG-A11 applies with r=2r=2. At q=1/2q=1/2,

RG,H(s,1/2)∼C2(2s−1)−3/32. R_{G,H}(s,1/2)\sim C_2(2s-1)^{-3/32}.

The arithmetic conclusion is exact. Its local source is also elementary: MG−MH=2q4(1−q)2M_G-M_H=2q^4(1-q)^2. Thus this example illustrates arithmetic visibility of degree-assortativity information. It does not demonstrate that volume two captures a fundamentally higher-order graph relation. Matching more demanding invariants is a separate task, and the interpretation of a collision should state precisely which invariants were matched.

7.3 A volume-three witness beyond the binary census

At volume three, the profile types are 3ev3e_v, 2eu+ev2e_u+e_v with u≠vu\ne v, and indicators of three-element subsets. Hence

ℓG,3(q)=∑vq9dv+∑u≠vq4du+dv−4Auv+∑|S|=3q|∂S|. \ell_{G,3}(q)=\sum_vq^{9d_v} +\sum_{u\ne v}q^{4d_u+d_v-4A_{uv}} +\sum_{|S|=3}q^{|\partial S|}. \tag{7.8}

This identity keeps the explanation transparent. The last term is binary. The middle term tests unequal heights at two vertices. It can distinguish a joint degree-mixing pattern that the degree-sum polynomial merges. Every energy remains a sum of pairwise edge terms; a later observation order does not introduce a new three-body interaction.

Calculation SNG-A13 — binary-census reference pair. Take

E(G)={03,04,06,12,13,23,24,35},E(H)={01,04,06,15,16,26,36,45}. \begin{aligned} E(G)&=\{03,04,06,12,13,23,24,35\},\\ E(H)&=\{01,04,06,15,16,26,36,45\}. \end{aligned}

Both have degree multiset {4,3,3,2,2,1,1}\{4,3,3,2,2,1,1\}. The exact finite binary census agrees for every subset size and cut size. The local coefficients agree through volume two, but their volume-three difference is

$$ \begin{aligned} \delta_3(q)={}&q^3-q^4-2q^6+2q^8+q^9+3q^{10} -3q^{11}-q^{12}-2q^{13}\\ &+2q^{15}+q^{17}-q^{18}\\ ={}&q^3(1-q)^5(1+q)^2 (1+2q+5q^2+6q^3+8q^4\\ &\hspace{38mm}+6q^5+5q^6+2q^7+q^8). \end{aligned} \tag{7.9} $$

The factorization proves positivity throughout 0<q<10<q<1; it is not a numerical sign test. At q=1/2q=1/2, the discrepancy is 11025/26214411025/262144. Therefore

RG,H(s,1/2)∼C3(3s−1)−11025/262144(s↓1/3). R_{G,H}(s,1/2) \sim C_3(3s-1)^{-11025/262144} \qquad(s\downarrow1/3). \tag{7.10}

The finite calculation can be reproduced without a symbolic algebra system. Generate every weak composition of volumes zero through three into seven labeled coordinates, evaluate the integer energy from the supplied edges, and accumulate multiplicities by energy. There are only 1,7,28,841,7,28,84 profiles at those volumes. Subtract the two energy histograms. Multiplication of the explicit factors in (7.9) independently checks the polynomial identity. The full binary claim requires the separate exhaustive census of 272^7 subsets; it is not inferred from the first four height coefficients.

This pair does not match the full joint degree table on edges. Its degree-sum polynomial agrees, but the more refined table does not. Consequently the witness proves that the unequal-height sector carries information beyond the aggregated binary census. It does not prove survival after every degree-assortativity statistic has been matched. A stronger search should match that full table as well and seek discrepancies at volume four or later. The first-discrepancy theorem will still apply; the difficult new work is finding and interpreting the local witness.

7.4 Effective control of the finite-prime approximation

A singularity law is more useful when its regular factor can be bounded rather than merely named. The following bounds require only local coefficient estimates and ordinary convergent sums. They do not require assumptions about prime gaps or an unproved asymptotic formula for primes.

For an integer cutoff P≥2P\ge2, define Z≤PZ_{\le P} by retaining primes at most PP. For real s>1s>1, put ρ=P−s<1\rho=P^{-s}<1. Since

0≤logL(t,q)≤L(t,q)−1≤kt(1−ρ)k+1(0≤t≤ρ), 0\le\log L(t,q)\le L(t,q)-1 \le\frac{kt}{(1-\rho)^{k+1}} \qquad(0\le t\le\rho),

we obtain the explicit interval

0≤logZG(s,q)−logZ≤P(s,q)≤k(1−ρ)k+1P1−ss−1. 0\le\log Z_G(s,q)-\log Z_{\le P}(s,q) \le\frac{k}{(1-\rho)^{k+1}} \frac{P^{1-s}}{s-1}. \tag{7.11}

Here the tail over primes was bounded by the tail over all integers, followed by the integral test. Exponentiating gives a multiplicative enclosure. The bound is deliberately conservative near s=1s=1, where raw Euler products converge slowly.

For the regularized ratio factor a faster bound is available. Set An=(n+k−1k−1)A_n=\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}, choose 0<ρ<10<\rho<1, and define the explicit nonnegative constants

D=(1−ρ)−k−1ρ,T=2ρr+1((1−ρ)−k−∑n=0rAnρn), D=\frac{(1-\rho)^{-k}-1}{\rho},\qquad T=\frac{2}{\rho^{r+1}} \left((1-\rho)^{-k}-\sum_{n=0}^{r}A_n\rho^n\right),

C=T+|δ|D+|δ|ρr−12(1−ρr). C=T+|\delta|D+ \frac{|\delta|\rho^{r-1}}{2(1-\rho^r)}. \tag{7.12}

Theorem SNG-A14 — computable regularized tail. Under the assumptions of Theorem SNG-A11, if real s>1/(r+1)s>1/(r+1) and P−s≤ρP^{-s}\le\rho, then

|logKG,H(s,q)−logKG,H,≤P(s,q)|≤CP1−(r+1)s(r+1)s−1. \left|\log K_{G,H}(s,q)-\log K_{G,H,\le P}(s,q)\right| \le C\frac{P^{1-(r+1)s}}{(r+1)s-1}. \tag{7.13}

Proof. Write A=LG(t,q)A=L_G(t,q), B=LH(t,q)B=L_H(t,q), and Dt=A−BD_t=A-B. Matching the coefficients below rr gives

|Dt−δtr|≤Ttr+1,max(A−1,B−1)≤Dt. |D_t-\delta t^r|\le Tt^{r+1},\qquad \max(A-1,B-1)\le Dt.

Because A,B≥1A,B\ge1,

logA−logB=∫01DtB+uDtdu. \log A-\log B=\int_0^1\frac{D_t}{B+uD_t}\,du.

The denominator is at least one. Subtracting δtr\delta t^r therefore gives an error at most (T+|δ|D)tr+1(T+|\delta|D)t^{r+1}. Finally

|log(1−tr)+tr|≤t2r2(1−ρr)≤ρr−1tr+12(1−ρr). |\log(1-t^r)+t^r| \le\frac{t^{2r}}{2(1-\rho^r)} \le\frac{\rho^{r-1}t^{r+1}}{2(1-\rho^r)}.

Adding these estimates bounds the absolute logarithm of one regularized factor by Ctr+1Ct^{r+1}. Sum over primes beyond PP, enlarge to all integers, and apply the integral test. ▫\square

The constant (7.12) is implemented exactly as regularized_tail_constant in src/singularity/arithmetic.py. Its proof uses only 0≤ℓn(q)≤An0\le\ell_n(q)\le A_n, valid for q∈[0,1]q\in[0,1], and t≤ρ<1t\le\rho<1. The older routine normalized_ratio_tail_constant bounds the same quantity through the coefficient ℓ1\ell^1 norm of the logarithm. It requires U=(1−ρ)−k−1<1U=(1-\rho)^{-k}-1<1 and is far weaker: for the binary pair at q=1/2q=1/2 and ρ=1/32\rho=1/32 it gives about 6.9×1056.9\times10^5, against about 451451 from (7.12). Both are retained, and (7.12) is preferred. For rational s=a/bs=a/b the cutoff is taken as P=NbP=N^b, so the tail bound CP1−(r+1)s/((r+1)s−1)CP^{1-(r+1)s}/((r+1)s-1) and the radius condition P−s=N−a≤ρP^{-s}=N^{-a}\le\rho are exact rational statements. Primes p≤Pp\le P are kept exactly in the finite product, and those beyond it satisfy p−s<ρp^{-s}<\rho. At s=1/rs=1/r the bound is Cr/NCr/N. The function certified_tail_record recomputes rr and δ\delta from the two supplied coefficient prefixes at the chosen qq before it produces a bound. It records the remaining hypotheses explicitly, refuses a prefix that ends before the discrepancy, and refuses a parameter such as q=1q=1 at which the discrepancy vanishes. The retained records for the three reference pairs at q=1/2q=1/2 are in results/tail_records.json. A test also checks the local inequality for the spectral pair at three rational points t≤ρt\le\rho, using rigorous rational enclosures of both local series by (7.14) and of (1−tr)δ(1-t^r)^\delta by Bernoulli’s inequalities, with no floating point.

The disc is explicit and very small. complex_disc_certificate in src/singularity/arithmetic.py checks (a)–(c) exactly, using the rational bounds 2−σ≤2−1/r(1+η)2^{-\sigma}\le2^{-1/r}(1+\eta) and e>27/10e>27/10. Theorem SNG-F39 (normalized local factors are entire). Let GG be connected on n≥2n\ge2 vertices with diameter DD, and fix 0<q<10<q<1. Then BG(t,q)=(1−tn)LG(t,q)B_G(t,q)=(1-t^n)L_G(t,q) is an entire function of tt, and LG(t,q)L_G(t,q) is meromorphic in tt, with poles at most at the nn-th roots of unity. For every H≥0H\ge0 and complex tt, |BG(t,q)−BG,≤H(t,q)|≤∑h>HNn(h)max(|t|h,|t|(n−1)h)q⌈h2/D⌉,Nn(h)=(h+1)n−2hn+(h−1)n, \bigl|B_G(t,q)-B_{G,\le H}(t,q)\bigr|\le\sum_{h>H}N_n(h)\,\max(|t|^h,|t|^{(n-1)h})\,q^{\lceil h^2/D\rceil},\qquad N_n(h)=(h+1)^n-2h^n+(h-1)^n, where BG,≤HB_{G,\le H} sums over minimum-zero profiles of maximum at most HH.

Proof. A minimum-zero profile of maximum hh has a vertex at height 00 and one at hh, joined by a path of at most DD edges. Cauchy–Schwarz along that path gives h2≤DEG(a)h^2\le D\,E_G(a). Its volume lies in [h,(n−1)h][h,(n-1)h], and Nn(h)N_n(h) counts the profiles in {0,…,h}n\{0,\ldots,h\}^n with minimum 00 and maximum hh, by inclusion–exclusion. This proves the tail bound. A profile of volume mm has h≥m/(n−1)h\ge m/(n-1), so |[tm]BG|≤(m+n−1n−1)qm2/((n−1)2D)|[t^m]B_G|\le\binom{m+n-1}{n-1}q^{m^2/((n-1)^2D)}. Hence |[tm]BG|1/m→0|[t^m]B_G|^{1/m}\to0, and the radius of convergence is infinite. ▫\square

For disconnected graphs the zero-energy profiles that are constant on components give BG(t,0)B_G(t,0)-type poles at roots of unity of the component sizes (SNG-F19), so connectedness is necessary. The theorem concerns one local factor at fixed qq. It says nothing about continuation of the product over primes.

Theorem SNG-F38 (certified enclosure of the regularized product). Under SNG-A11 with G,HG,H connected and q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1) rational, fix rational s=a/bs=a/b with (r+1)s>1(r+1)s>1, an integer NN, the cutoff P=NbP=N^b and ρ=N−a=P−s\rho=N^{-a}=P^{-s}. T'=\sum_{r<n\le M}|\ell_n-m_n|\rho^{n-r-1}+\frac{2S_M}{\rho^{r+1}},\qquad D'=\sum_{1\le n\le M}\max(\ell_n,m_n)\rho^{n-1}+\frac{S_M}\rho,\qquad C'=T'+|\delta|D'+\frac{|\delta|\rho^{r-1}}{2(1-\rho^r)} . src/singularity/certified.py implements the theorem with 256 fractional bits. The minimum-zero condition is carried as a flag in the bag messages, so no subtraction of enclosures occurs. For t=p−a/bt=p^{-a/b} the factor (1−tr)(1-t^r) is exact when b∣rab\mid ra, in particular at s=1/rs=1/r. The retained results are in results/certified_k.json. For the spectral pair at q=1/2q=1/2 and s=1/2s=1/2, with all 12291229 primes below 10410^4 kept, the interval for logK\log K has width below 10−210^{-2}. Local factors themselves can also be enclosed by finitely many height coefficients. If LN(t,q)=∑n=0Nℓn(q)tnL_N(t,q)=\sum_{n=0}^N\ell_n(q)t^n, choose any t<R<1t<R<1. Then

0≤L(t,q)−LN(t,q)≤(t/R)N+1(1−R)−k. 0\le L(t,q)-L_N(t,q) \le (t/R)^{N+1}(1-R)^{-k}. \tag{7.14}

Indeed each omitted term gains at most (t/R)N+1(t/R)^{N+1}, and the complete series at RR is bounded by (1−R)−k(1-R)^{-k}. Since LN≥1L_N\ge1, its logarithmic error is at most the same bound. Finite-prime and finite-height errors can thus be propagated separately and added in logarithmic coordinates. A numerical implementation claiming a rigorous enclosure must also bound its arithmetic rounding; the inequalities alone do not certify an unchecked floating-point product.

These results establish controllable local witnesses, arithmetic visibility, and finite approximation. They leave a genuine open inverse question: which graph distinctions are invisible to the entire univariate volume-marked local series? The examples show strict separations from specified coarser observations. They do not answer that complete question or establish historical priority for the construction.

The distinction also lies in a specific span sector. Volume-three profiles of the form 3ev3e_v have span three and agree because degrees agree.
