7.6 A secondary boundary layer at an endpoint

The first-discrepancy exponent itself can become small near an endpoint. This produces a second controlled scaling law, now for graph ratios rather than the original synchronized partition function.

Theorem SNG-A20 — endpoint scaling of visibility. Suppose the polynomial local coefficients of two graphs agree below volume rr for every q∈[0,1]q\in[0,1]. Let q*∈[0,1]q_*\in[0,1] be a value where the entire local series agree, and write δ(q)=ℓG,r(q)−ℓH,r(q)\delta(q)=\ell_{G,r}(q)-\ell_{H,r}(q). Let qj→q*q_j\to q_*, εj↓0\varepsilon_j\downarrow0, with

δ(qj)log(1/εj)→τ∈ℝ. \delta(q_j)\log(1/\varepsilon_j)\longrightarrow\tau\in\mathbb R.

Then

RG,H((1+εj)/r,qj)→eτ. R_{G,H}((1+\varepsilon_j)/r,q_j)\longrightarrow e^\tau. \tag{7.15}

Proof. The normalized local ratio in (7.3) has its first rr nonconstant coefficients canceled identically in qq. Its O(xr+1)O(x^{r+1}) estimate can be chosen uniformly on the compact weight interval. Therefore the regularized prime product is jointly continuous near (1/r,q*)(1/r,q_*), by uniform convergence of the large-prime logarithmic tail and positivity of the finitely many remaining factors. At q*q_*, every local ratio is one and δ(q*)=0\delta(q_*)=0, so K(1/r,q*)=1K(1/r,q_*)=1. Finally

logR=δ(qj)logζ(1+εj)+logK. \log R=\delta(q_j)\log\zeta(1+\varepsilon_j)+\log K.

The second term tends to zero, while logζ(1+ε)−log(1/ε)→0\log\zeta(1+\varepsilon)-\log(1/\varepsilon)\to0 and δ\delta stays bounded. This proves the limit. ▫\square

For the volume-two pair, δ2(q)∼4(1−q)3\delta_2(q)\sim4(1-q)^3 as q↑1q\uparrow1. For the volume-three pair, δ3(q)∼144(1−q)5\delta_3(q)\sim144(1-q)^5, because the final polynomial factor in (7.9) has value 36 at one. Thus (1−q)5log(1/ε)→t(1-q)^5\log(1/\varepsilon)\to t yields the ratio limit e144te^{144t} for the second pair at s=(1+ε)/3s=(1+\varepsilon)/3. Near zero the corresponding leading behaviors are δ2∼2q2\delta_2\sim2q^2 and δ3∼q3\delta_3\sim q^3. These are proved parameter scales for particular exact witnesses. They do not establish a universal exponent for all graph pairs.

8 Synchronization limits, uniform scaling, and exact contractions

Setting the energy weight to zero and letting the arithmetic size parameter approach its divergence point are different operations. At zero weight a connected graph forces every coordinate integer to agree, producing ζ(ks)\zeta(ks). At any fixed positive weight the system has rare unequal valuations at every prime, and their combined contribution diverges at s=1s=1. There are infinitely many opportunities for a rare local event. A small penalty need not remain negligible when those opportunities accumulate. This chapter turns that intuition into a uniform theorem and then develops optional extensions that retain the same exact arithmetic meaning.

Assume first that GG is connected with k≥2k\ge2, minimum degree d≥1d\ge1, and edge connectivity λ≥1\lambda\ge1. Write mdm_d for the number of vertices of degree dd, and α(q)=∑vqdv\alpha(q)=\sum_vq^{d_v}. All limits below use real positive parameters. No complex continuation is needed for the double-scaling statements.

8.1 An explicit estimate uniform in the energy weight

We begin with constants that are intentionally simple rather than optimized. Define

Dk=2(2k−1),Ck=4(2k−1−k/2),Ak=Ck+Dk2/2+k. D_k=2(2^k-1),\qquad C_k=4(2^k-1-k/2),\qquad A_k=C_k+D_k^2/2+k. \tag{8.1}

Let

Jk=∑n≥2lognnk<∞. J_k=\sum_{n\ge2}\frac{\log n}{n^k}<\infty.

This last constant is computable with an elementary integral remainder. For a cutoff N≥2N\ge2, the omitted tail is at most

∫N∞logttkdt=N1−k(logNk−1+1(k−1)2). \int_N^\infty\frac{\log t}{t^k}\,dt =N^{1-k}\left(\frac{\log N}{k-1}+\frac1{(k-1)^2}\right). \tag{8.2}

The summand is decreasing on [2,∞)[2,\infty) for k≥2k\ge2, so the integral bound applies directly.

Theorem SNG-A15 — uniform synchronization estimate. For 0≤q≤10\le q\le1 and ε>0\varepsilon>0,

$$ \begin{aligned} &\left|\log Z_G(1+\varepsilon,q) -\log\zeta(k)-\alpha(q)\log(1/\varepsilon)\right|\\ &\hspace{12mm}\le A_kq^\lambda\bigl(\zeta(2)-1\bigr) +(kJ_k+k)\varepsilon. \end{aligned} \tag{8.3} $$

Proof. Write BG(x,q)=1+u(x,q)B_G(x,q)=1+u(x,q). Every nonzero minimum-zero profile has energy at least λ\lambda. Therefore, for real 0≤x≤1/20\le x\le1/2,

0≤u(x,q)≤qλDkx, 0\le u(x,q)\le q^\lambda D_kx,

and, since the volume-one coefficient is α(q)\alpha(q),

0≤u(x,q)−α(q)x≤qλCkx2. 0\le u(x,q)-\alpha(q)x\le q^\lambda C_kx^2.

To verify the constants, bound each minimum-zero coefficient by the number of all weak compositions. At x≤1/2x\le1/2, dividing the first bound by xx and the second by x2x^2 leaves geometric-composition sums bounded respectively by DkD_k and CkC_k. These bounds discard graph information but retain the crucial factor qλq^\lambda.

For u≥0u\ge0, integration of 1−1/(1+u)1-1/(1+u) gives

0≤u−log(1+u)≤u2/2. 0\le u-\log(1+u)\le u^2/2.

Also |log(1−x)+x|≤x2/[2(1−x)]|\log(1-x)+x|\le x^2/[2(1-x)], and α(q)≤kqλ\alpha(q)\le kq^\lambda. Combining the estimates gives

|logBG(x,q)+α(q)log(1−x)|≤Akqλx2. |\log B_G(x,q)+\alpha(q)\log(1-x)| \le A_kq^\lambda x^2. \tag{8.4}

Here q2λ≤qλq^{2\lambda}\le q^\lambda was used in the quadratic term. Substitute x=p−sx=p^{-s}, with real s≥1s\ge1, and sum over primes. By common-shift factorization,

logHG(s,q)−logζ(ks)=∑p{logBG(p−s,q)+α(q)log(1−p−s)}. \log H_G(s,q)-\log\zeta(ks) =\sum_p\{\log B_G(p^{-s},q)+\alpha(q)\log(1-p^{-s})\}.

Thus its absolute value is at most Akqλ(ζ(2)−1)A_kq^\lambda(\zeta(2)-1). The derivative bound |(logζ)′(t)|≤∑n≥2(logn)n−k=Jk|(\log\zeta)'(t)|\le\sum_{n\ge2}(\log n)n^{-k}=J_k for t≥kt\ge k gives

|logζ(k(1+ε))−logζ(k)|≤kJkε. |\log\zeta(k(1+\varepsilon))-\log\zeta(k)|\le kJ_k\varepsilon.

Finally the integral test yields 1/ε≤ζ(1+ε)≤1+1/ε1/\varepsilon\le\zeta(1+\varepsilon)\le1+1/\varepsilon. Hence

0≤logζ(1+ε)−log(1/ε)≤ε. 0\le\log\zeta(1+\varepsilon)-\log(1/\varepsilon) \le\varepsilon.

Multiply by α(q)≤k\alpha(q)\le k, use the leading factorization, and add the three error bounds. ▫\square

This proof provides more than continuity of a regular factor. It shows exactly which uniform estimate permits the two parameters to move together. The graph-dependent minimum-cut exponent controls the error in replacing the regular factor by its synchronized value. The minimum-degree exponent will control the rare unequal valuations that are amplified by the singular factor. Those exponents need not be equal, and they play different mathematical roles.

8.2 The double-scaling law

Theorem SNG-A16 — synchronization boundary layer. Let qj→0q_j\to0, εj↓0\varepsilon_j\downarrow0. If

α(qj)log(1/εj)→τin [0,∞], \alpha(q_j)\log(1/\varepsilon_j)\longrightarrow\tau \quad\text{in }[0,\infty],

then

ZG(1+εj,qj)→ζ(k)eτ, Z_G(1+\varepsilon_j,q_j) \longrightarrow\zeta(k)e^\tau, \tag{8.5}

where e+∞=+∞e^{+\infty}=+\infty. In particular, if

qjdlog(1/εj)→t<∞, q_j^d\log(1/\varepsilon_j)\longrightarrow t<\infty,

then the limit is ζ(k)emdt\zeta(k)e^{m_dt}. If that product tends to infinity, the partition function tends to infinity.

Proof. The error in (8.3) tends to zero. Exponentiating gives the first statement, including the infinite case. For the second, use

α(q)=mdqd+R(q),0≤R(q)≤(k−md)qd+1. \alpha(q)=m_dq^d+R(q),\qquad 0\le R(q)\le(k-m_d)q^{d+1}.

When qdlog(1/ε)q^d\log(1/\varepsilon) has a finite limit, the extra contribution R(q)log(1/ε)R(q)\log(1/\varepsilon) tends to zero. In the infinite case, α(q)≥mdqd\alpha(q)\ge m_dq^d is enough. ▫\square

The scaling variable is logarithmic in the distance to the arithmetic singularity. For a graph with minimum degree one, maintaining a nontrivial finite limit requires qq of order 1/log(1/ε)1/\log(1/\varepsilon). With minimum degree two it requires order 1/log(1/ε)1/\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}. This is a conclusion of the exact estimate, not a power-law ansatz chosen from numerical plots. The coefficient mdm_d counts the cheapest single-vertex disagreements.

The theorem also explains the noncommuting iterated limits. At fixed ε>0\varepsilon>0, sending q→0q\to0 gives ζ(k(1+ε))\zeta(k(1+\varepsilon)), and then sending ε→0\varepsilon\to0 gives ζ(k)\zeta(k). At fixed q>0q>0, sending ε→0\varepsilon\to0 gives infinity, so subsequently shrinking qq does not recover that finite iterated limit. A family can therefore look synchronized throughout a large finite range and still have a different limiting divergence. The double-scaling variable states how close to one the size parameter must be before that discrepancy matters.

8.3 Optional extension: vertex masses

Positive integer vertex masses allow exact contraction without pretending that a merged vertex represents only one original coordinate. Assign a mass mv≥1m_v\ge1 to each vertex and let M=∑vmvM=\sum_vm_v. Define

LG,m(x,q)=∑a≥0qEG(a)x∑vmvav. L_{G,m}(x,q)=\sum_{a\ge0}q^{E_G(a)}x^{\sum_vm_va_v}.

Its arithmetic counterpart weights an integer tuple by ∏vnv−mvs\prod_vn_v^{-m_vs}. All coefficients remain finite, and a common shift increases weighted volume by MM.

Theorem SNG-A17 — weighted endpoints and first divergence. For connected GG,

LG,m=BG,m1−xM,ZG,m(s,0)=ζ(Ms),ZG,m(s,1)=∏vζ(mvs). L_{G,m}=\frac{B_{G,m}}{1-x^M},\quad Z_{G,m}(s,0)=\zeta(Ms),\quad Z_{G,m}(s,1)=\prod_v\zeta(m_vs).

Let r=minvmvr=\min_vm_v and fix 0<q≤10<q\le1. Put γ(q)=∑mv=rqdv\gamma(q)=\sum_{m_v=r}q^{d_v}. Then the first nonconstant local term is γ(q)xr\gamma(q)x^r, the Euler product converges for real s>1/rs>1/r, and

ZG,m(s,q)=ζ(rs)γ(q)HG,m(s,q), Z_{G,m}(s,q)=\zeta(rs)^{\gamma(q)}H_{G,m}(s,q),

with a positive nonzero regular factor near s=1/rs=1/r. Therefore its leading real singular exponent there is γ(q)\gamma(q).

Proof. The shift and endpoint arguments are unchanged after adding masses. The least positive weighted volume is rr, attained exactly by the profiles eve_v with mv=rm_v=r. Their energies are dvd_v. Every remaining weighted volume is an integer at least r+1r+1. Multiplication by (1−xr)γ(q)(1-x^r)^{\gamma(q)} leaves 1+O(xr+1)1+O(x^{r+1}), and the same proof as Theorem SNG-A11 gives the regular factor. At least one vertex has minimum mass and q>0q>0, so γ(q)>0\gamma(q)>0; logarithmic divergence at s=1/rs=1/r also proves the sharp real convergence threshold. ▫\square

This extension changes the arithmetic size observable while retaining the same graph energy. It need not be interpreted as adding physical masses. Its exact purpose is to remember how many original coordinates have been identified, or how strongly their integer sizes are weighted. Ignoring those weights after contraction would move the synchronized zeta factor to the wrong argument.

8.4 Optional extension: partial edge synchronization

Allow one energy weight qe∈[0,1]q_e\in[0,1] for every edge. The local weight is ∏eqe(au−av)2\prod_eq_e^{(a_u-a_v)^2}. Setting a selected edge weight to zero imposes equality of its endpoint heights. Equality propagates through the connected components of the selected-edge subgraph.

Theorem SNG-A18 — exact contraction under zero edge weights. Let F⊆EF\subseteq E, and set qe=0q_e=0 for e∈Fe\in F. Let C1,…,CtC_1,\ldots,C_t be the components of (V,F)(V,F). Replace each component by one vertex of mass |Ci||C_i|. An unselected edge between CiC_i and CjC_j contributes its original factor qe(bi−bj)2q_e^{(b_i-b_j)^2}; an internal unselected edge contributes one. Then the resulting weighted, possibly multiple-edge local series equals the original specialized local series exactly. The equality also holds for the Euler products on every common domain of absolute convergence.

Proof. A profile survives the zero weights exactly when it is constant on each CiC_i. Such profiles correspond bijectively to b∈ℤ≥0tb\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^t. Its original volume is ∑i|Ci|bi\sum_i|C_i|b_i. Internal edges have zero difference, and every remaining edge retains its stated difference and weight. This is equality term by term. Euler assembly follows on an absolutely convergent domain. ▫\square

Parallel surviving edges can be combined: their weights multiply, since q1d2q2d2=(q1q2)d2q_1^{d^2}q_2^{d^2}=(q_1q_2)^{d^2}. Their presence is therefore supported mathematically even if the core graph class remains simple. The contraction description is an optional extended representation, not a request to accept duplicate edges silently in the ordinary constructor.

Contraction order does not matter. Applying zero constraints in stages produces the equivalence relation generated by all selected edges. Vertex masses add associatively, internal edges disappear, and external weights multiply associatively. This is a direct consequence of the termwise bijection, not an appeal to an unspecified categorical equivalence. If the selected edges connect the entire graph, the result is one vertex of mass kk, recovering ζ(ks)\zeta(ks).

One can retain separate complex size parameters svs_v as well. A synchronized component then has parameter sCi=∑v∈Cisvs_{C_i}=\sum_{v\in C_i}s_v. A sufficient domain before contraction is ℜsv>1\Re s_v>1 for every vertex; after contraction the less restrictive sufficient condition is ℜsCi>1\Re s_{C_i}>1 for every component. The exact local identity remains valid wherever the relevant sums converge. This multivariate refinement records how contraction redistributes size exponents without claiming a complete several-variable continuation theory.

8.5 Positive ordering and probabilistic derivatives

There is a further useful consequence of retaining positive weights. If G⊆HG\subseteq H on the same vertex set, then EH(a)≥EG(a)E_H(a)\ge E_G(a). Hence, for q∈[0,1]q\in[0,1], every local coefficient and every real convergent arithmetic value satisfies LH≤LGL_H\le L_G and ZH≤ZGZ_H\le Z_G. Adding constraints reduces the positive population weight. The corresponding ratio need not be monotone in ss, and no such stronger ordering is asserted.

For real s>1s>1 and q=e−βq=e^{-\beta}, normalize the integer-tuple weights by ZGZ_G. This defines an ordinary probability distribution. Its sufficient statistics are U(n)=log∏vnvU(n)=\log\prod_vn_v and V(n)=ℰG(n)V(n)=\mathcal E_G(n). On compact parameter sets with s>1s>1 and β≥0\beta\ge0, all their polynomial moments are finite. Differentiating gives

∂slogZ=−𝔼[U],∂βlogZ=−𝔼[V], \partial_s\log Z=-\mathbb E[U],\qquad \partial_\beta\log Z=-\mathbb E[V],

∇(s,β)2logZ=(Var(U)Cov(U,V)Cov(U,V)Var(V))≽0. \nabla^2_{(s,\beta)}\log Z =\begin{pmatrix}\operatorname{Var}(U)&\operatorname{Cov}(U,V)\\ \operatorname{Cov}(U,V)&\operatorname{Var}(V)\end{pmatrix}\succeq0. \tag{8.6}

To justify finiteness, note that local energy is at most a graph-dependent constant times squared local volume, while the local geometric coefficient majorant has every polynomial volume moment at p−sp^{-s}. Summing their prime contributions and logarithmic size factors is uniformly convergent when ss stays above one. Alternatively, global energy is bounded by a constant times (log∏vnv)2(\log\prod_vn_v)^2, and products of powers of logarithms remain summable against ∏vnv−s\prod_vn_v^{-s}. Dominated differentiation follows. The covariance identity is a general property of a normalized exponential family, used here with an explicitly defined arithmetic population.

These derivative identities supply rigorous sensitivity observations. They do not add a physical interpretation, empirical model, or claim of a thermodynamic phase transition. The proved limiting phenomenon is the uniform arithmetic boundary layer in Theorem SNG-A16. Its higher-order corrections, sharp graph-dependent constants, and possible multivariate visibility geometries remain separate analytic research questions.

8.6 A worked contraction sequence

Take the four-vertex path 0−1−2−30-1-2-3, initially with mass one at every vertex and a common positive edge weight qq. Its leading exponent at s=1s=1 is 2q+2q22q+2q^2, because its endpoint degrees are one and its internal degrees are two. Now set the weight on edge 0101 to zero while retaining weight qq on the other edges. The surviving local profiles are exactly (a,a,b,c)(a,a,b,c), and their local series is

∑a,b,c≥0x2a+b+cq(a−b)2+(b−c)2. \sum_{a,b,c\ge0}x^{2a+b+c} q^{(a-b)^2+(b-c)^2}. \tag{8.7}

The contracted path has masses 2,1,12,1,1. Its light vertices have degrees two and one, so Theorem SNG-A17 gives leading exponent q2+qq^2+q at s=1s=1. The heavy vertex is still part of the graph energy, but it cannot occur in the lowest-volume profile. This is why simply counting contracted vertices would give the wrong answer.

Next synchronize edge 2323 as well. The surviving profiles are (a,a,b,b)(a,a,b,b). There are two contracted vertices, each of mass two, joined by the original middle edge. The local factor is exactly LK2(x2,q)L_{K_2}(x^2,q), and its arithmetic product is ZK2(2s,q)Z_{K_2}(2s,q). The first divergence moves to s=1/2s=1/2, with exponent 2q2q. Finally synchronize the middle edge; all four heights become equal and the product becomes ζ(4s)\zeta(4s), whose first divergence is at s=1/4s=1/4.

The changes in threshold have a direct combinatorial explanation. A minimal positive shift of a synchronized block raises every original coordinate in that block. Its arithmetic denominator is therefore the corresponding power of an integer, rather than the first power associated with a single original vertex. The contraction operation preserves that information through its masses. The example also shows why a statement about an exactly zero coupling should not be inferred from small positive couplings without a uniform estimate: rare violations of the equality constraint can restore a divergence at a different location.

For the derivative identities (8.6), values at β=0\beta=0 mean derivatives from the allowed side β≥0\beta\ge0. At an interior value β>0\beta>0, ordinary derivatives are available in a neighborhood. The one-sided convention is necessary because rewarding unbounded quadratic energy with β<0\beta<0 makes even a local height series diverge. This is a domain issue in the mathematical definition, not a numerical instability that can be fixed by increasing a cutoff.

9 Exact examples: what the new population distinguishes

This chapter records the finite evidence on which the first release rests. The examples are deliberately small enough that their defining populations can be examined without numerical approximation. They serve a precise purpose: to show that integer heights retain relational information that certain familiar summaries discard. They do not establish that the resulting invariant determines every graph, that the Euler product adds information to its local factor, or that the construction has historical priority. The claims below distinguish direct arguments from exact finite computations. The computations can be repeated through the standard-library package accompanying this manuscript.

Throughout the chapter a graph is simple, undirected, and has the labeled vertex set V={0,1,…,6}V=\{0,1,\ldots,6\}. Labels specify the input and the assignments being counted. The resulting polynomials are unchanged by relabeling the graph, because a permutation of vertices induces a bijection on all height assignments. An edge written 0303 means the unordered pair {0,3}\{0,3\}. The height energy is

EG(a)=∑{i,j}∈E(G)(ai−aj)2,|a|=∑iai. E_G(a)=\sum_{\{i,j\}\in E(G)}(a_i-a_j)^2, \qquad |a|=\sum_i a_i.

The unnormalized local population and the normalized marked population are

PG(x,q)=∑a∈ℕ7x|a|qEG(a), P_G(x,q)=\sum_{a\in\mathbb N^7}x^{|a|}q^{E_G(a)},

BG(x,q,z)=∑a∈ℕ7miniai=0x|a|qEG(a)zmaxiai. B_G(x,q,z)=\sum_{\substack{a\in\mathbb N^7\\\min_i a_i=0}} x^{|a|}q^{E_G(a)}z^{\max_i a_i}.

Volume means total integer height. The variable zz records height span after the common minimum has been removed. Consequently BG(x,q,1)=(1−x7)PG(x,q)B_G(x,q,1)=(1-x^7)P_G(x,q). For volumes below seven, the coefficients of the unmarked normalized and unnormalized series agree. Every assignment of such a volume already has a zero coordinate. This observation lets us discuss the first local coefficients and their span decomposition without changing normalization halfway through an argument.

9.1 Two different comparisons

The first pair has equal Laplacian spectra. The second pair has equal complete binary cut-volume populations. These are separate examples, and keeping them separate prevents an unsupported inference about a single pair defeating every existing invariant.

All four graphs are connected. Each spectral graph has one triangle and four bridges. Each binary graph has the same two-connected block, a theta graph with three internally disjoint paths of lengths one, two, and three, together with two attached bridges. The attachments differ. This distinction between a common block structure and different vertex attachments will matter when we compare the marked population with an ordinary cut-lattice theta series.

Proposition SNG-E001: the spectral graphs are nonisomorphic. Each graph has a unique vertex of degree four, namely vertex zero. In GspG_{\mathrm{sp}}, that vertex lies in the triangle 0,1,20,1,2. In HspH_{\mathrm{sp}}, the only triangle is 1,5,61,5,6, which excludes vertex zero. An isomorphism preserves vertex degrees and triangle membership. It would therefore have to send the degree-four vertex to the degree-four vertex while preserving a property that differs, which is impossible.

Proposition SNG-E002: the binary graphs are nonisomorphic. The unique degree-four vertex of GbinG_{\mathrm{bin}} is vertex three, and its neighbors are 0,1,2,50,1,2,5. Exactly one of these neighbors, vertex five, is a leaf. The unique degree-four vertex of HbinH_{\mathrm{bin}} is vertex six, with neighbors 0,1,2,30,1,2,3. Exactly two of those neighbors are leaves. The number of leaf neighbors of a specified degree class is invariant under isomorphism. The graphs are therefore nonisomorphic.

These short arguments are logically independent of the population computation. A differing graph invariant would also prove nonisomorphism, but an elementary structural witness makes the examples easier to inspect. It also guards against a mistaken interpretation in which a relabeling of one graph has merely been counted in a different order.

9.5 What the analytic signatures see

For the primewise Euler lift, the singularity exponent at s=1s=1 is the common degree polynomial cG(q)=∑iqdic_G(q)=\sum_iq^{d_i}. Accordingly neither pair is distinguished by that leading exponent. The spectral pair shares

csp(q)=3q+2q2+q3+q4, c_{\mathrm{sp}}(q)=3q+2q^2+q^3+q^4,

and the binary pair shares

cbin(q)=2q+2q2+2q3+q4. c_{\mathrm{bin}}(q)=2q+2q^2+2q^3+q^4.

Both zero-parameter Euler products are ζ(7s)\zeta(7s), because all four graphs are connected. The first minimum-cut correction also agrees within each pair. For the spectral graphs, the oriented minimum-cut side sizes occur with multiplicities three, one, one, three at sizes one, three, four, six. For the binary graphs only sizes one and six occur, each twice. If 𝒫(s)=∑pp−s\mathcal P(s)=\sum_pp^{-s}, the respective first corrections to log(ZG/ζ(7s))\log(Z_G/\zeta(7s)) are

q(3𝒫(s)+𝒫(3s)+𝒫(4s)+3𝒫(6s)) q\bigl(3\mathcal P(s)+\mathcal P(3s)+\mathcal P(4s)+3\mathcal P(6s)\bigr)

and

2q(𝒫(s)+𝒫(6s)). 2q\bigl(\mathcal P(s)+\mathcal P(6s)\bigr).

Those common signatures illustrate why a hierarchy is necessary. A graph can share degree data, a leading singular exponent, and its entire minimum-cut volume census with another graph while differing at a later local coefficient. After cancellation of the lower equal local coefficients, the first ratio singularity occurs at s=1/2s=1/2 for the spectral pair and s=1/3s=1/3 for the binary pair. Its exponent is respectively 2q2(1−q)3(1+q)2q^2(1-q)^3(1+q) or Δ(q)\Delta(q). This is a local continuation statement on the positive-real branch for the ratio after cancellation; it is not a blanket meromorphic continuation of either original product.

The finite evidence supports a sharply bounded conclusion. The height-span marked invariant is strictly finer than its binary sector, and its unmarked specialization can distinguish a displayed Laplacian-cospectral pair. Both examples also distinguish vertex realizations with isometric ordinary cut lattices. The evidence does not prove completeness, does not show that the unmarked series always recovers the binary sector, and does not establish an efficient algorithm for general graph isomorphism. What has been established is a concrete, exact relational distinction and an analytic language that records where that distinction first appears.

9.6 A regular calibration: the cube and the Möbius ladder

A third comparison tests the low-volume blindness of regular graphs proved in the inverse-problems chapter. Let Q3Q_3 be the cube graph on binary vertex labels 0,…,70,\ldots,7, with an edge whenever two labels differ in one binary digit. Let M8M_8 be the eight-cycle together with the four opposite-vertex chords. Their edge sets are fixed here to make the computation reproducible.

Graph Edge set

Both graphs have eight vertices, twelve edges, degree three at every vertex, and no triangles. They are nonisomorphic for a simple reason. The cube is bipartite: the parity of the number of ones in the binary label changes across every edge. The ladder contains the five-cycle 0,1,2,3,4,00,1,2,3,4,0, using its opposite chord 0404, and therefore is not bipartite. No spectral calculation is needed for that nonisomorphism witness.

The common local coefficients through volume three are

A0=1,A1=8q3, A_0=1,\qquad A_1=8q^3,

Their span decompositions also agree. This agreement is predicted by the theorem that order, regular degree and triangle count determine the marked coefficients through volume three. It is therefore a mathematically controlled delay, rather than an unexplained failure of the population calculation. At volume four the binary subsets already distinguish the graphs:

The six cube subsets of boundary size four are its six square faces. Its two four-vertex subsets of boundary size twelve are its bipartition classes, each containing no internal edges. The ladder has no such boundary-twelve four-subset, consistently with the absence of a bipartition into independent four-sets. The other coefficients count the remaining labeled subsets, rather than quotienting them by graph symmetries.

[x4](PQ3−PM8)=[x4z](BQ3−BM8)=2q4(1−q2)4. [x^4](P_{Q_3}-P_{M_8}) =[x^4z](B_{Q_3}-B_{M_8}) =\boxed{2q^4(1-q^2)^4}.

Their status is exact finite computation, followed by exact polynomial factorization. The first ratio singularity of this pair is at s=1/4s=1/4, with exponent 2q4(1−q2)42q^4(1-q^2)^4, after the equal lower-volume terms are cancelled. The common leading exponent at s=1s=1 is 8q38q^3.

This pair is not another collision of the complete binary polynomial. It agrees only in the early coefficients and separates in a binary sector at volume four. The nonbinary discrepancy at volume five adds an example of how span information is distributed, but is not needed to distinguish the graphs once the binary four-subset census is available. Its role is calibration: it demonstrates a predicted limitation of very early coefficients and provides a positive check that the next level responds to a concrete structural difference.

9.7 Reading the examples as a controlled experiment

The two pairs answer related but different objections. One might first suspect that the construction is simply a complicated way to reproduce the eigenvalues of a graph Laplacian. The spectral pair rules out that interpretation: the entire Laplacian characteristic polynomial agrees, while a positive difference appears at volume two for every interior real parameter. One might then suspect that the extra information is entirely the familiar information obtained by considering all binary cuts and remembering their side sizes. The binary pair rules out that second interpretation: every binary coefficient agrees, while a positive difference appears in the next height span. The experimental sequence is therefore a sequence of exact controls, not a ranking based on a few numerical scores.

The controls are intentionally strong within their stated scope. Both pairs have the same degree multiset, so a singleton degree statistic cannot explain either separation. Both also share their number of components, spanning-tree count, edge connectivity and minimum-cut volume census. Those equalities do not make the examples universally difficult. A simple neighborhood statistic separates each pair, and the second pair has different Laplacian spectra. The point is to identify a definite piece of information that the height population retains, not to pretend that no other mathematical description can retain it.

For the binary pair, the first additional statistic is particularly transparent. An ordered pair (i,j)(i,j) receives heights two and one. Its energy is 4di+dj−4ϵij4d_i+d_j-4\epsilon_{ij}. A binary pair only sees di+dj−2ϵijd_i+d_j-2\epsilon_{ij}, without distinguishing which endpoint is emphasized. The complete binary triple census adds many constraints, but it still does not force the displayed ordered-pair energy distribution. The table supplies a direct counterexample. The new information is a degree and adjacency mixing statistic that is visible through an asymmetric height pattern and is then aggregated without labels.

The analytic ratio does not create that statistic. It transports an already established local discrepancy into a location on the real singularity ladder. The spectral pair first differs at an exponent sum of two and therefore has its first ratio singularity at one half. The binary pair first differs at an exponent sum of three and therefore has its first ratio singularity at one third. This interpretation is helpful because it connects a combinatorial order of distinction to an analytic scale, while keeping the logical direction clear: the exact coefficient calculation comes first, and the analytic statement follows from it.

10 Inverse problems and the depth of a height population

An invariant is a way of asking questions about an object while discarding its presentation. The inverse problem asks how much of the object can be recovered from the answers. For relational height populations, this question must be posed at several levels. A finite depth, the full marked series, an unmarked specialization, and a primewise Euler product are different data structures. Their relationships can be proved in some directions and remain open in others. Confusing them would replace a promising research question with an unsupported completeness claim.

The purpose of this chapter is to define those relationships and identify useful targets. The small examples show that the construction preserves some information absent from binary cut populations and the Laplacian spectrum. They do not tell us how many nonisomorphic graphs remain indistinguishable. In particular, a hierarchy can improve at one level and still stabilize long before it becomes complete. Determining whether that happens is a central mathematical task, rather than a detail to be deferred until after a universal reconstruction claim.

10.1 Which equivalence is being studied?

Fix the number of vertices nn. Graphs are considered up to ordinary graph isomorphism, but every coefficient counts assignments on the original vertex set before relabeling. Let

BG(x,q,z)=∑mina=0x|a|qEG(a)zmaxa B_G(x,q,z)=\sum_{\min a=0}x^{|a|}q^{E_G(a)}z^{\max a}

be the normalized marked series. We say that G≡markHG\equiv_{\mathrm{mark}}H when these formal series agree. We say that G≡unmarkHG\equiv_{\mathrm{unmark}}H when their specializations at z=1z=1 agree. The latter is equivalent to equality of the unnormalized local series PGP_G for graphs of the same order, because BG(x,q,1)=(1−xn)PG(x,q)B_G(x,q,1)=(1-x^n)P_G(x,q). These are definitions, not claims that either relation is graph isomorphism.

For an integer D≥0D\ge0, define the depth-DD population by

BG≤D(x,q,z)=∑h=0Dzh[zh]BG(x,q,z). B_G^{\le D}(x,q,z)=\sum_{h=0}^{D}z^h[z^h]B_G(x,q,z).

Equality of these finite polynomials is written G≡DHG\equiv_DH. The depth is the largest height span retained; it is not the total volume and is not an iteration count in a numerical algorithm. For fixed DD, every coordinate lies between zero and DD, at least one coordinate is zero, and the number of assignments is exactly (D+1)n−Dn(D+1)^n-D^n. Thus each depth comparison is a finite exact question.

Proposition SNG-I001: hierarchy implications. Graph isomorphism implies marked equality. Marked equality implies equality at every finite depth and implies unmarked equality. Equality at depth D+1D+1 implies equality at depth DD. Conversely, equality at every finite depth implies equality of the full marked series, because every individual coefficient has a finite span. These statements follow directly from coefficient extraction and specialization. No converse from unmarked equality to marked equality is asserted.

The first depth is precisely the binary cut sector, after its two constant assignments are restored. If

CG(x,q)=∑S⊆Vx|S|q|∂S|, C_G(x,q)=\sum_{S\subseteq V}x^{|S|}q^{|\partial S|},

then

CG(x,q)=1+xn+[z]BG(x,q,z). C_G(x,q)=1+x^n+[z]B_G(x,q,z). \tag{SNG-I002}

The term one is the empty subset and the term xnx^n is the full subset. Both have zero boundary. The normalized span-one population excludes them because a representative must attain both zero and one. The binary pair in the preceding chapter agrees at depth one and differs at depth two, proving that this particular hierarchy step is strict. This is a theorem about the defined hierarchy, supported by an exact counterexample to equality of its first two levels.

For two graphs define their first marked distinguishing depth by

dspan(G,H)=min{D:G≢DH}, d_{\mathrm{span}}(G,H)=\min\{D:G\not\equiv_DH\},

with value infinity when no finite depth distinguishes them. One may separately define a first distinguishing volume by the smallest rr at which a coefficient of xrx^r differs. The two measures answer different questions. A large span can be concentrated on one vertex, while a low span can involve many vertices. The binary pair has distinguishing span two and distinguishing volume three. Its difference at volume three belongs specifically to span two; it is not evidence that every depth-two distinction must first occur at volume three.

10.2 Why retaining labels makes reconstruction easy

The intended inverse problem is difficult because vertex labels have been summed out. It is important to explain why a seemingly stronger multivariate formulation would trivialize part of that question. Define the fully labeled local series

𝒫G(x1,…,xn;q)=∑a∈ℕnqEG(a)∏ixiai. \mathscr P_G(x_1,\ldots,x_n;q) =\sum_{a\in\mathbb N^n}q^{E_G(a)}\prod_i x_i^{a_i}.

Its singleton coefficient is [xi]𝒫G=qdi[x_i]\mathscr P_G=q^{d_i}, so it determines the degree of every named vertex. Its coefficient at two distinct variables is

[xixj]𝒫G=qdi+dj−2ϵij. [x_ix_j]\mathscr P_G=q^{d_i+d_j-2\epsilon_{ij}}.

The exponent therefore reveals whether the named pair is an edge. This proves Proposition SNG-I003: the labeled formal series determines the entire labeled graph using coefficients of total degree at most two. A formal parameter avoids questions of numerical recognition. At a fixed exact real q∈(0,1)q\in(0,1), the distinct integer powers are also distinct, but a floating-point implementation should not be substituted for that exact statement without an error analysis.

This easy reconstruction is not the problem Singularity is claiming to solve. The specialization x1=⋯=xn=xx_1=\cdots=x_n=x combines many assignments into one volume class. Individual pair identities disappear, and their relational distribution remains. The challenge is to recover a graph from that distribution without quietly reintroducing one coordinate variable per vertex. This distinction also explains why a large formal generating function need not supply an efficient isomorphism algorithm. One can encode the adjacency matrix in a generating function almost immediately; the mathematical question is what survives a specified loss of labels.

10.3 Universal relations within each depth

Several identities are available before any difficult inverse problem is solved. They constrain every valid output and reveal how the hierarchy is organized. They also provide exact checks that are different from merely running the same enumeration twice.

Proposition SNG-I004: span reflection. Put BG,h(x,q)=[zh]BG(x,q,z)B_{G,h}(x,q)=[z^h]B_G(x,q,z). Then

BG,h(x,q)=xnhBG,h(x−1,q). B_{G,h}(x,q)=x^{nh}B_{G,h}(x^{-1},q).

For a normalized assignment of span hh, the reflected assignment a′i=h−aia'_i=h-a_i again has minimum zero and maximum hh. Every edge difference changes sign, so energy is unchanged, while volume becomes nh−|a|nh-|a|. Reflection is an involution, proving the identity coefficient by coefficient. For h=1h=1, this is the usual complement symmetry of binary cuts. For the seven-vertex binary pair, its proved x3z2x^3z^2 difference therefore also occurs at x11z2x^{11}z^2, since 14−3=1114-3=11. This second location follows from a bijection, not from a new empirical claim.

For h≥1h\ge1, an assignment of exact span hh has at least one coordinate zero and at least one equal to hh. Consequently its volume lies between hh and (n−1)h(n-1)h. Its energy is an integer between zero and |E|h2|E|h^2. If the graph is connected and h>0h>0, the energy is positive. These bounds make BG,hB_{G,h} a finite polynomial with explicitly bounded support. The reflection center nh/2nh/2 is consistent with the two volume bounds.

There is an inclusion-exclusion construction that does not require enforcing minimum and maximum conditions separately in a transfer algorithm. Define

TG,h(x,q)=∑a∈{0,…,h}nx|a|qEG(a),TG,−1=0. T_{G,h}(x,q)=\sum_{a\in\{0,\ldots,h\}^n}x^{|a|}q^{E_G(a)}, \qquad T_{G,-1}=0.

For h≥1h\ge1, shift invariance of energy gives

BG,h=TG,h−(1+xn)TG,h−1+xnTG,h−2. B_{G,h}=T_{G,h}-(1+x^n)T_{G,h-1}+x^nT_{G,h-2}. \tag{SNG-I005}

Assignments missing the top height contribute TG,h−1T_{G,h-1}. Assignments missing zero can be shifted down by one, contributing xnTG,h−1x^nT_{G,h-1}. Assignments missing both endpoints have been subtracted twice and contribute xnTG,h−2x^nT_{G,h-2}. The formula holds for every graph because only common-shift invariance was used. At q=1q=1, it reduces to a universal volume polynomial independent of graph edges. In particular,

BG,h(1,1)=(h+1)n−2hn+(h−1)n. B_{G,h}(1,1)=(h+1)^n-2h^n+(h-1)^n.

Summing through depth DD gives (D+1)n−Dn(D+1)^n-D^n, as required. At unmarked q=1q=1, one obtains the further check

BG(x,1,1)=1−xn(1−x)n. B_G(x,1,1)=\frac{1-x^n}{(1-x)^n}.

These identities explain why all examples coincide when energy is forgotten. A successful distinguishing polynomial must vanish at that specialization. They also clarify why a zero at q=1q=1 is a necessary population constraint, rather than evidence by itself of a special physical or cyclotomic mechanism.

10.4 Connected components and exact recovery at zero parameter

Disconnected graphs require a different normalization argument from connected graphs. Energy zero means that height is constant on each connected component, not that all vertices share a common height. If the component sizes are n1,…,ncn_1,\ldots,n_c, then

PG(x,0)=∏j=1c11−xnj,ZG(s,0)=∏j=1cζ(njs). P_G(x,0)=\prod_{j=1}^c\frac1{1-x^{n_j}}, \qquad Z_G(s,0)=\prod_{j=1}^c\zeta(n_js). \tag{SNG-I006}

This statement follows by assigning an arbitrary nonnegative common height to each component. It includes isolated vertices, whose factors are (1−x)−1(1-x)^{-1} and ζ(s)\zeta(s). It shows why the connected-graph claim that the zero-parameter value is finite at s=1s=1 cannot be copied unchanged to a graph with isolated vertices.

Proposition SNG-I007: the zero-parameter local series determines the multiset of component sizes. Let mdm_d be the number of components of size dd, and put br=r[xr]logPG(x,0)b_r=r[x^r]\log P_G(x,0). Expanding the logarithm gives

br=∑d∣rdmd. b_r=\sum_{d\mid r}d\,m_d.

Möbius inversion yields

mn=1n∑d∣nμ(n/d)bd. m_n=\frac1n\sum_{d\mid n}\mu(n/d)b_d.

All operations here are formal power-series operations; no analytic continuation is needed. This recovers component sizes, not the internal graph on each component. Within a fixed connected component size, all connected graphs have the same zero-energy population.

For unmarked populations, ordinary disjoint union gives PG⊔H=PGPHP_{G\sqcup H}=P_GP_H. The globally normalized marked population does not simply factor as BGBHB_GB_H: the two components may be shifted by different heights before their common global minimum is removed, and the global span depends on those relative shifts. A depth algorithm must retain this information or work first with the bounded boxes TG,hT_{G,h}, which do multiply over disjoint components, and then use the inclusion-exclusion formula. Treating marked disjoint union as an automatic product would erase legitimate assignments.

10.5 Easy classes and the limits of degree information

The first local coefficient is the degree polynomial cG(q)=∑vqdvc_G(q)=\sum_vq^{d_v}. It determines the degree multiset, because its coefficient of qdq^d is the number of degree-dd vertices. This immediately resolves several inverse questions under explicit class assumptions. Such small results are useful calibration points; they must not be expanded into a claim about arbitrary graphs with the same degree sequence.

For a star K1,n−1K_{1,n-1},

cG(q)=(n−1)q+qn−1. c_G(q)=(n-1)q+q^{n-1}.

For a path PnP_n with n≥3n\ge3,

cG(q)=2q+(n−2)q2. c_G(q)=2q+(n-2)q^2.

The two polynomials differ for n≥4n\ge4, while the three-vertex star and path are the same graph. A degree multiset consisting of one degree-n−1n-1 vertex and n−1n-1 leaves forces the star even without a prior star-family promise. A connected graph whose vertices all have degree two is a cycle, so the degree polynomial determines it within that connected class. If connectedness is omitted, a disjoint union of cycles has the same degree polynomial for every partition of the total order into allowed cycle lengths. The zero-parameter component-size series then resolves those different cycle decompositions.

A connected tree of maximum degree at most two is a path: there can be no branch and no cycle. Complete graphs and edgeless graphs are also forced by their degree multisets. Within the family of complete bipartite graphs, the polynomial aqb+bqaa q^b+b q^a determines the unordered pair of part sizes {a,b}\{a,b\}. This last statement has a family restriction. Other graph families may share that degree sequence, so the polynomial by itself does not certify complete bipartiteness.

The early coefficients become less informative on regular graphs. If GG is dd-regular on nn vertices with m=nd/2m=nd/2, then

A2=nq4d+mq2d−2+((n2)−m)q2d. A_2=nq^{4d}+m q^{2d-2} +\left(\binom n2-m\right)q^{2d}.

Thus no two dd-regular graphs of the same order can be distinguished at volume two. At volume three, the ordered 2+12+1 sector is

2mq5d−4+(n(n−1)−2m)q5d. 2m q^{5d-4}+\bigl(n(n-1)-2m\bigr)q^{5d}.

The remaining binary triple sector depends on the numbers NjN_j of three-vertex subsets spanning exactly jj edges. If T=N3T=N_3 is the triangle count, then

N2+3T=n(d2),N1+2N2+3T=m(n−2), N_2+3T=n\binom d2, \qquad N_1+2N_2+3T=m(n-2),

N0+N1+N2+T=(n3). N_0+N_1+N_2+T=\binom n3.

These identities count wedges, edge-containing triples, and all triples. They show that n,d,Tn,d,T determine every NjN_j. Therefore Proposition SNG-I008 states that regular graphs with the same order, degree and triangle count have identical marked coefficients through total volume three. This result supplies a useful negative prediction for searches. The heterogeneous degrees of the displayed binary pair are part of why an ordered height pattern can distinguish it so early.

There are also useful support bounds on the coefficients at arbitrary volume. Suppose the graph is connected on n≥2n\ge2 vertices, with maximum degree dmax>0d_{\max}>0 and edge connectivity λ\lambda. For a nonnegative assignment of volume rr,

EG(a)=∑idiai2−2∑ij∈Eaiaj≤dmax∑iai2≤dmaxr2. E_G(a)=\sum_i d_i a_i^2-2\sum_{ij\in E}a_ia_j \le d_{\max}\sum_i a_i^2\le d_{\max}r^2.

The upper bound is attained by placing all height rr at a maximum-degree vertex. For r≥1r\ge1, equality in ∑iai2≤r2\sum_i a_i^2\le r^2 requires that only one coordinate be positive. Therefore the coefficient of the highest possible energy qdmaxr2q^{d_{\max}r^2} in [xr]PG[x^r]P_G is exactly the number of maximum-degree vertices. This is Proposition SNG-I009, an exact boundary constraint on every local population. It should not be mistaken for a new distinguishing statistic: it is already determined by the first coefficient’s degree data.

For a normalized nonzero assignment, let h=maxah=\max a. The threshold-cut identity and integrality give EG(a)≥λhE_G(a)\ge\lambda h. At least one coordinate is zero, so r≤(n−1)hr\le(n-1)h. Consequently every occupied coefficient of the normalized population at positive volume satisfies

EG(a)≥λ⌈rn−1⌉. E_G(a)\ge\lambda\left\lceil\frac r{n-1}\right\rceil.

This lower bound is easy to evaluate and does not require solving an optimization problem over all assignments. It is not asserted to be sharp at every volume. A spectral bound can be stronger at large volume: if λ2\lambda_2 is the first nonzero Laplacian eigenvalue, subtract the mean of aa to obtain

EG(a)≥λ2(∑iai2−r2n)≥λ2r2n(n−1). E_G(a)\ge\lambda_2\left(\sum_i a_i^2-\frac{r^2}n\right) \ge\frac{\lambda_2r^2}{n(n-1)}.

The last step follows because a zero coordinate leaves at most n−1n-1 nonzero coordinates and Cauchy’s inequality gives ∑iai2≥r2/(n−1)\sum_i a_i^2\ge r^2/(n-1). These inequalities connect familiar spectral control to the support of the new population without equating the two objects. They help delimit an exact search region, while the examples show that knowledge of the spectrum does not determine the multiplicities within that region.

10.6 A family with exactly controlled visibility depth

The decorated-deck criterion SNG-F17 asks whether nonisomorphic graphs can agree through arbitrarily large volume. They can, with an explicit discrepancy. For ℓ≥2\ell\ge2 and 1≤j≤ℓ1\le j\le\ell, let Gℓ,jG_{\ell,j} be the cycle C2ℓC_{2\ell} on 0,…,2ℓ−10,\ldots,2\ell-1 with a leaf uu attached at vertex 00 and a leaf ww attached at vertex jj. The graphs have n=2ℓ+2n=2\ell+2 vertices, the same degree sequence and the same multiset of endpoint-degree types on edges when j≥2j\ge2. Their cut lattices are isometric: each is the cut lattice of C2ℓC_{2\ell} orthogonally summed with ℤ2\mathbb Z^2 for the two pendant edges, whose differences are free. So the energy theta series that forgets volume is identical. They are not cospectral in general.

Theorem SNG-F36 (exact visibility depth for pendant cycles). For 2≤p<ℓ2\le p<\ell, the graphs Gℓ,pG_{\ell,p} and Gℓ,ℓG_{\ell,\ell} have equal local, normalized and span-marked coefficients at every volume m≤pm\le p, and [xp+1](LGℓ,p−LGℓ,ℓ)=q2(1−q)2(1−q2)p. [x^{p+1}]\bigl(L_{G_{\ell,p}}-L_{G_{\ell,\ell}}\bigr)=q^2(1-q)^2(1-q^2)^p . The discrepancy at volume p+1p+1 lies entirely in span one. More precisely, the complete binary-sector difference is ∑S⊆Vz|S|(qcGℓ,p(S)−qcGℓ,ℓ(S))=q2(1−q)2(1−q2)pzp+1(1−z)2Uℓ−p(z,q)2, \sum_{S\subseteq V}z^{|S|}\bigl(q^{c_{G_{\ell,p}}(S)}-q^{c_{G_{\ell,\ell}}(S)}\bigr) =q^2(1-q)^2(1-q^2)^p\,z^{p+1}(1-z)^2\,U_{\ell-p}(z,q)^2, where U0=0U_0=0, U1=1U_1=1 and Uk=(1+z)Uk−1−z(1−q2)Uk−2U_k=(1+z)U_{k-1}-z(1-q^2)U_{k-2}. The binary formula holds for 1≤p<ℓ1\le p<\ell.

Proof. Binary sector. Summing over the leaves first: if its attachment vertex is outside SS, a leaf contributes 1+zq1+zq; if inside, q+z=(1+zq)−(1−q)(1−z)q+z=(1+zq)-(1-q)(1-z). Write ϕ(s)=ϕ0−(1−q)(1−z)s\phi(s)=\phi_0-(1-q)(1-z)s for s∈{0,1}s\in\{0,1\}. With N=2ℓN=2\ell, T=(1qzqzz)T=\begin{pmatrix}1&q\sqrt z\\ q\sqrt z&z\end{pmatrix} and Π=diag(0,1)\Pi=\operatorname{diag}(0,1), the cycle part of the binary polynomial with both vertices 00 and jj in SS is Γ(j)=tr(ΠTjΠTN−j)\Gamma(j)=\operatorname{tr}(\Pi T^j\Pi T^{N-j}). Terms with fewer marked vertices in SS do not depend on jj, by rotation and reflection of the cycle. Hence the difference is (1−q)2(1−z)2(Γ(p)−Γ(ℓ))(1-q)^2(1-z)^2(\Gamma(p)-\Gamma(\ell)). With orthonormal eigenvectors v±v_\pm and eigenvalues λ±\lambda_\pm of TT, Γ(j)=∑a,b∈{±}(va)22(vb)22λajλbN−j. \Gamma(j)=\sum_{a,b\in\{\pm\}}(v_a)_2^2(v_b)_2^2\lambda_a^j\lambda_b^{N-j}. The diagonal terms do not depend on jj, and (v+)22(v−)22=β2/(λ+−λ−)2(v_+)_2^2(v_-)_2^2=\beta^2/(\lambda_+-\lambda_-)^2 for the off-diagonal entry β=qz\beta=q\sqrt z. So Γ(p)−Γ(ℓ)=q2z(λ+−λ−)2(λ+pλ−N−p+λ−pλ+N−p−2(λ+λ−)ℓ)=q2z(λ+λ−)pUℓ−p2, \Gamma(p)-\Gamma(\ell)=\frac{q^2z}{(\lambda_+-\lambda_-)^2}\bigl(\lambda_+^p\lambda_-^{N-p}+\lambda_-^p\lambda_+^{N-p}-2(\lambda_+\lambda_-)^\ell\bigr) =q^2z\,(\lambda_+\lambda_-)^pU_{\ell-p}^2, with λ+λ−=detT=z(1−q2)\lambda_+\lambda_-=\det T=z(1-q^2) and Uk=(λ+k−λ−k)/(λ+−λ−)U_k=(\lambda_+^k-\lambda_-^k)/(\lambda_+-\lambda_-). This satisfies the stated recurrence, since λ++λ−=1+z\lambda_++\lambda_-=1+z. Since Uk=1+O(z)U_k=1+O(z), the lowest term is q2(1−q)2(1−q2)pzp+1q^2(1-q)^2(1-q^2)^pz^{p+1}.

Decorated decks of size at most pp. Let SS have t≤pt\le p vertices. Each component of Gℓ,j[S]G_{\ell,j}[S] is either an isolated leaf whose attachment vertex is outside SS, or an arc of the cycle with the leaves of its marked vertices that lie in SS. An arc containing both marked vertices would need at least p+1p+1 cycle vertices for j=pj=p and ℓ+1\ell+1 for j=ℓj=\ell, so each arc contains at most one. The degree-decorated type of SS is therefore a multiset of components of three kinds: free arcs, which contain no marked vertex and are recorded by their lengths; marked arcs, recorded by length, the offset of the degree-three vertex and whether its leaf is present; and isolated leaves. The two marked vertices are interchangeable, each having degree three and one leaf. Fix a type τ\tau and an assignment of its marked components to the two marked vertices; then the marked arcs are placed. The free arcs, of total length FF in kk blocks, must be placed pairwise non-adjacent, avoiding the marked vertices and non-adjacent to the marked arcs, in the two segments between the marked regions. Let α1,α2\alpha_1,\alpha_2 be the segment lengths after removing one obligatory gap next to each marked arc. Placing labeled blocks in one segment of effective length α\alpha has k!(α−F+1k)k!\binom{\alpha-F+1}{k} solutions up to the labeling convention, so the two-segment count is a sum over splits of the blocks of products of binomials.

Placement lemma. This sum is a function of α1+α2\alpha_1+\alpha_2 alone whenever α1,α2≥F−1\alpha_1,\alpha_2\ge F-1. Gluing the segments with one separator vertex identifies the count with placements in a line of length α1+α2+1\alpha_1+\alpha_2+1, which depends only on the sum, minus placements in which some block covers the separator. The latter decompose, block by block and offset by offset, into the same two-segment problem with one block fewer. By induction on kk, the count is a function of the sum once both lengths are at least FF. As a polynomial identity in (α1,α2)(\alpha_1,\alpha_2) it then holds everywhere. For αi≥F−1\alpha_i\ge F-1 every binomial (αi−FI+1|I|)\binom{\alpha_i-F_I+1}{|I|} has a nonnegative upper argument, so it equals the true count.

For Gℓ,ℓG_{\ell,\ell} both segments come from arcs with ℓ−1≥p\ell-1\ge p interior vertices. For Gℓ,pG_{\ell,p} the short arc has p−1p-1 interior vertices, and the marked arcs remove at most (t−F)(t-F) of them together with their gaps, so α1≥p−1−(t−F)≥F−1\alpha_1\ge p-1-(t-F)\ge F-1; the long arc is larger. The same counting shows that the marked arcs fit in both graphs whenever t≤pt\le p. The sum α1+α2\alpha_1+\alpha_2 depends only on τ\tau and the assignment, so both graphs have the same number of subsets of each decorated type and size t≤pt\le p.

Conclusion. SNG-F17 gives equality of local and marked coefficients through volume pp. At volume p+1p+1, its proof matches every profile whose support has at most pp vertices. The remaining profiles have p+1p+1 support vertices and volume p+1p+1, so they are binary. Their difference is the zp+1z^{p+1} coefficient above, and these subsets are proper because p+1<np+1<n. ▫\square

Taking ℓ=p+1\ell=p+1 gives n=2p+4n=2p+4 and visibility depth p+1=(n−2)/2p+1=(n-2)/2, linear in the order. The theorem is unconditional and explicit, and it answers the first question raised after SNG-F17. It is not a uniform statement about all graph pairs of a given order.

Theorem SNG-F37 (sign and monotonicity of the pendant discrepancy). For real 0<x<10<x<1 and 0<q<10<q<1, and 1≤j≤j′≤ℓ1\le j\le j'\le\ell, LGℓ,j(x,q)≥LGℓ,j′(x,q). L_{G_{\ell,j}}(x,q)\ge L_{G_{\ell,j'}}(x,q).

Proof. Let f(h)=∑b≥0xbq(b−h)2f(h)=\sum_{b\ge0}x^bq^{(b-h)^2} be the leaf factor, bounded by 1/(1−x)1/(1-x). Let TT be the operator on ℓ2(ℤ≥0)\ell^2(\mathbb Z_{\ge0}) with kernel x(h+h′)/2q(h−h′)2x^{(h+h')/2}q^{(h-h')^2}. It is Hilbert–Schmidt, and it is positive semidefinite because q(h−h′)2=e−c(h−h′)2q^{(h-h')^2}=e^{-c(h-h')^2} with c=−logq>0c=-\log q>0 is a positive-definite Gaussian kernel, and conjugating by the diagonal xh/2x^{h/2} preserves this. 10.7 Terminal kernels and the Whitney twist

A block is a graph GG with an ordered tuple 𝐬=(s1,…,sk)\mathbf s=(s_1,\ldots,s_k) of distinct terminal vertices. Write I=V\𝐬I=V\setminus\mathbf s. Its terminal kernel is the family of series KG(𝐛;x,q)=∑aI≥0x∑i∈IaiqEG(aI,𝐛),𝐛∈ℤ≥0k, K_G(\mathbf b;x,q)=\sum_{a_I\ge0}x^{\sum_{i\in I}a_i}\,q^{E_G(a_I,\mathbf b)},\qquad\mathbf b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^k, where EG(aI,𝐛)E_G(a_I,\mathbf b) is the energy of the profile equal to 𝐛\mathbf b on the terminals and to aIa_I inside. Kernels retain terminal heights and interior volume separately, so they compose.

Theorem SNG-F41 (gluing and the Whitney twist). Let (G1,𝐬)(G_1,\mathbf s) and (G2,𝐭)(G_2,\mathbf t) be blocks with kk terminals that share no edge, and let G1∪πG2G_1\cup_\pi G_2 identify sis_i with tπ(i)t_{\pi(i)} for a permutation π\pi. For k=2k=2, put Aj(b1,b2)=12(KGj(b1,b2)−KGj(b2,b1))A_j(b_1,b_2)=\frac12\bigl(K_{G_j}(b_1,b_2)-K_{G_j}(b_2,b_1)\bigr). Then the straight and twisted gluings satisfy LG1∪G2−LG1∪twG2=2∑𝐛x|𝐛|A1(𝐛)A2(𝐛). In particular the twist is invisible at every volume if either kernel is symmetric, for instance if a block has an automorphism exchanging its terminals.

The pendant-cycle family is an instance. Let Bm,kB_{m,k} be the path of length 2m2m from ss to tt with a leaf at distance k<mk<m from ss. Gluing it to itself gives C4mC_{4m} with leaves 2k2k apart, and the twist gives leaves 2m2m apart. These are G2m,2kG_{2m,2k} and G2m,2mG_{2m,2m} of SNG-F36. SNG-F42 then gives depth 2k+12k+1 and leading coefficient q2(1−q)2(1−q2)2kq^2(1-q)^2(1-q^2)^{2k}, in agreement with SNG-F36, and its positivity is the even case of SNG-F37. The kernel point of view separates the mechanism from the family. Proposition SNG-F43 (marked composition). For blocks as in SNG-F41, let K(H)K^{(H)} be the box kernel, with every height, terminals included, in {0,…,H}\{0,\ldots,H\}. Global marks are not local: the minimum and maximum of a glued profile may sit in either block, so the marked series cannot be read from the unbounded kernels alone. The box kernels supply exactly the missing information. marked_glue in src/singularity/terminals.py implements this, and the tests compare it with direct marked enumeration for straight and twisted gluings and for a disconnected block.

In the ring ℚ(q)[x]/(xR+1)\mathbb Q(q)[x]/(x^{R+1}), or ℚ[x]/(xR+1)\mathbb Q[x]/(x^{R+1}) after specializing qq, the differences f(h)−f(h′)≡qh2−qh′2(modx)f(h)-f(h')\equiv q^{h^2}-q^{h'^2}\pmod x are units for h≠h′h\ne h', because their constant terms are nonzero (for 0<q0<10<q_0<1 the numbers q0h2q_0^{h^2} are distinct). The tensor Vandermonde matrix (∏if(bi)ri)𝐫,𝐛\bigl(\prod_if(b_i)^{r_i}\bigr)_{\mathbf r,\mathbf b}, with 𝐛,𝐫∈{0,…,R}k\mathbf b,\mathbf r\in\{0,\ldots,R\}^k, is therefore invertible: its determinant is a product of powers of these differences. Solving recovers every y𝐛y_{\mathbf b}, including those with |𝐛|>R|\mathbf b|>R, which vanish. The ‘if’ part of the consequence is the gluing formula; the ‘only if’ part follows from the star contexts. ▫\square

So every distinction a block can make in any context is already made by star contexts. The kernel is the complete interface object for edge-disjoint gluing at its terminals. Linear recovery needs at least as many probes as unknowns y𝐛y_{\mathbf b} with |𝐛|≤R|\mathbf b|\le R, namely (R+kk)\binom{R+k}{k}; the star family uses (R+1)k(R+1)^k. Whether a smaller realizable family suffices, and how much a restricted family of contexts can compress the interface, are the open questions of the proposed units P49–P54. recover_kernel_from_probes in src/singularity/terminals.py carries out the inversion at a rational q0q_0. The test recovers a two-terminal kernel through volume three from sixteen glued graphs counted by plain enumeration.

A twist changes the graph but preserves its cycle matroid, so the cut lattice and its energy theta series are unchanged. A block whose kernel is symmetric without an exchanging automorphism would therefore give two graphs with identical scalar height series. Among all connected blocks with at most five vertices and balanced terminals, the kernel through volume six is symmetric exactly when such an automorphism exists. This finite search does not decide the question in general. src/singularity/terminals.py computes kernels on a checked decomposition, with the terminals in every bag, and checks them against enumeration. tests/test_terminals.py verifies the gluing formulas for two and three terminals, the twist identity, invisibility for symmetric blocks, and the depth formula and identification above for Bm,kB_{m,k} with m≤4m\le4.

10.8 What should be searched next?

The first inverse question is whether full marked equality implies graph isomorphism on any substantial class. Trees are an attractive target because the ordinary cut lattice of every tree is a standard integer lattice and therefore discards almost all attachment geometry. The marked volume population could preserve some of that geometry. Completeness on trees is a question, not a conclusion. A single pair of nonisomorphic trees with equal full marked series would refute it; a finite census without a collision would only establish a bounded result.

A second question is whether the full hierarchy eventually stops improving on a fixed graph order. Since there are finitely many isomorphism classes on nn vertices, if the full marked invariant is complete on that order then some finite maximum distinguishing depth exists. This existence is purely finite and does not supply a useful bound. If the invariant has collisions, the same argument instead gives a finite depth at which its equivalence partition stabilizes to its final, possibly nontrivial partition. A search can record that stabilization for a finite census, while a theorem must control all higher depths.

A third question concerns the loss of the span marker. It is possible that the unmarked series is complete on a class where no simple proof recovers the binary sector. It is also possible that different marked populations collapse to the same unmarked series. Neither possibility is settled by the current examples. The appropriate experiment compares marked equality and unmarked equality separately, rather than assuming that agreement or disagreement of one automatically decides the other.

A useful search ledger should retain graph order, component sizes, degree polynomial, binary profile, first different volume, first different span, and exact difference polynomial. It should separate pairs selected to collide under a background invariant from arbitrary pairs that happen to be easy to distinguish. Regular graphs with equal triangle count offer controlled difficult cases after the easy volume-three obstructions have been removed. Trees offer a different challenge, in which lattice isometry is automatic but attachment structure varies. Graphs related by changes of attachment within a common block structure test whether the volume marker preserves the intended vertex realization.

These are falsifiable targets. The hypothesis that depth two distinguishes all binary-profile collisions can be rejected by one depth-two collision. The hypothesis that a finite volume cutoff suffices for all graphs of a stated order needs a census whose completeness is itself justified. The hypothesis that a coefficient depends only on a known motif census can be tested by deriving its assignment patterns before scanning data. Every negative result would locate an exact limit of the representation. Such a limit would still be useful mathematics, because it would say what relational information the population has actually retained.

11 Archival bridges: what is inherited and what changes

Singularity did not arise from an empty mathematical landscape. PerfectPower, PerfectJet, the SOE program, and older conductor and lattice investigations already contain several of its ingredients. The appropriate historical claim is therefore narrow: the present project selects a different object and a different inverse question from a substantial existing toolkit. It does not claim to invent prime valuations, graph Laplacians, discrete Gaussian heights, cut lattices, binary Ising polynomials, or Euler products. Those established subjects are part of the mathematical background [BHN1997; AM2009; BPR2024]. The value of the new direction must be demonstrated through its precise marking, its exact examples, and the questions those examples make available.

This chapter explains the bridges in mathematical terms. A shared vocabulary such as population, shadow, quotient or phase is not enough to establish a bridge. There must be a defined map, a preserved quantity, an exact identity, or a specifically stated proposal. The distinction matters because the archives contain both successful computations and ambitious descriptions whose full objects were not implemented. Reusing a phrase should not silently upgrade the status of either the old claim or the new one.

11.1 From multiplicative integers to relational exponent geometry

The oldest relevant arithmetic step is the valuation embedding

n↦v(n)=(v2(n),v3(n),v5(n),…). n\longmapsto v(n)=(v_2(n),v_3(n),v_5(n),\ldots).

Every positive integer gives a finitely supported nonnegative integer vector, and multiplication becomes addition: v(mn)=v(m)+v(n)v(mn)=v(m)+v(n). The June collision work used this geometry to define

κ(m,n)=∑pvp(m)vp(n). \kappa(m,n)=\sum_pv_p(m)v_p(n).

It related shared prime support to a dot product and represented divisors of an integer as a product of finite chains. Its analytic deformation rewarded or penalized shared exponents with etκ(m,n)e^{t\kappa(m,n)}. The exact Euler factor was ∑a,b≥0etabp−s(a+b)\sum_{a,b\ge0}e^{tab}p^{-s(a+b)}. A positive real reward is unstable because the terms with a=b=Na=b=N contain quadratic exponential growth against only a linear exponential penalty. This is a specific mathematical limitation, not a general failure of the valuation viewpoint [PJ2026].

The present construction uses exponent differences instead of that attractive dot product. For a graph GG, put

ℰG(n1,…,nk)=∑p∑ij∈E(G)(vp(ni)−vp(nj))2. \mathcal E_G(n_1,\ldots,n_k) =\sum_p\sum_{ij\in E(G)}(v_p(n_i)-v_p(n_j))^2.

The sum is finite for every tuple because only finitely many primes divide the product. For 0≤q≤10\le q\le1, the weight qℰGq^{\mathcal E_G} is bounded by one. The resulting series is therefore dominated by the independent tuple series in its elementary convergence domain. This change does more than repair a divergent sign. It creates a zero-energy relation: two adjacent integer positions must have equal valuations at every prime, hence equal integers. On a connected graph, zero energy means the entire tuple is constant.

Proposition SNG-I020: exact synchronization at zero parameter. For a connected graph on kk vertices,

ℰG(n1,…,nk)=0⇔n1=⋯=nk. \mathcal E_G(n_1,\ldots,n_k)=0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n_1=\cdots=n_k.

The forward direction follows because each squared difference must vanish and equality propagates along graph paths. The reverse direction is immediate. For disconnected graphs, equality is required separately on each component. Thus the earlier multiplicative linearization now supports a relational arithmetic population. The graph specifies which exponent coordinates must agree; the primewise product turns that specification into a Dirichlet series.

There is no information gain in the Euler lift itself. Once PG(x,q)P_G(x,q) is known, ∏pPG(p−s,q)\prod_pP_G(p^{-s},q) is fixed in its convergence domain. Conversely, the coefficient of a prime power prp^r in the Dirichlet series recovers [xr]PG[x^r]P_G, because a product equal to prp^r forces every tuple entry to be a power of that single prime. The arithmetic series is an exact re-expression with useful analytic operations, not an additional sensor that distinguishes graphs whose full local factors agree.

11.2 From exact populations to navigable height assignments

PerfectPower repeatedly studies a large finite population through counts, conditional counts, rankings and samples instead of explicitly listing every member. That approach transfers directly to bounded height populations [PP2026]. At depth DD, the original objects are vectors a∈{0,…,D}ka\in\{0,\ldots,D\}^k with minimum zero. Their number is (D+1)k−Dk(D+1)^k-D^k. If energy, volume and span constraints are imposed, the retained population is smaller but remains a population of original assignments. A conditional count can determine how many completions remain after the first few coordinates have been fixed.

The released HeightPopulation supplies exact completion counts; lexicographic ranking and unranking follow from the usual branching identity. At a prefix uu, the total completion count is the sum of completion counts after each allowed next height. A rank selects the first branch whose cumulative count exceeds it. An original assignment receives a rank by adding all earlier branch populations. This supplies an exact navigation mechanism for height configurations without identifying assignments that merely share a profile. It also makes uniform sampling possible by drawing a uniform integer rank in the feasible population.

The distinction between counting assignments and counting profile types is essential. The energy-volume-span histogram may have relatively few occupied cells, but a cell’s coefficient is its multiplicity. Replacing that coefficient by one changes the invariant. The seven-vertex span-two cubic sector has forty-two ordered assignments even when only a modest set of energies occurs. Its successful distinction depends on the distribution of those multiplicities. The population machinery is therefore relevant as an exact computational method, while its prior application domains need not be imported into the present mathematical target.

An exact residual decomposition also becomes possible. A partial assignment contributes the energy of edges whose endpoints are both processed. Edges crossing to unprocessed vertices remain symbolic functions of their boundary heights. Their contributions should not be guessed from the already accumulated scalar energy. Keeping the boundary state allows future assignments to complete the squared differences exactly. This is the natural finite-state interface for dynamic programming over a path or tree decomposition. For a fixed cutoff DD, a boundary of size bb has at most (D+1)b(D+1)^b raw height states before any further reduction. This is a conditional complexity observation about a chosen decomposition, not a universal small-state theorem.

11.3 From all-future behavioral equivalence to weighted transfer states

The SOE program formalizes the principle that two partial states should be identified exactly when every allowed future continuation gives the same observable behavior [SOE2026]. A direct analog exists for a fixed finite height-transfer computation. The observation is now a polynomial population, and a continuation adds vertices, edges, weights, or terminal conditions according to a declared processing scheme. Two boundary states can be merged only when all continuations permitted by that scheme produce the same remaining generating polynomial.

That sentence is a proposed computational use of the SOE idea, not a claim that the previous Lean theorem has already verified this graph algorithm. Several details must be fixed before a formal transport is legitimate. The state must include any boundary heights required by future edges, the accumulated or deferred volume information, and sufficient data to enforce the global span convention. Polynomial weights must be handled over a specified coefficient structure. A quotient of a two-state partial machine does not automatically verify a family of graph transfers with arbitrarily many boundary states.

The proposal nevertheless has a concrete exact form. Let a processing alphabet encode the legal remaining transfer steps for a fixed decomposition. To a partial state ss, associate the function fs(w)f_s(w) giving the remaining polynomial after continuation word ww. Define s∼ts\sim t when fs(w)=ft(w)f_s(w)=f_t(w) for every permitted ww. This equivalence is correct by definition and is stable under a common legal next step. The research problem is to compute it efficiently and provide a finite certificate that the retained tests suffice. On a fixed finite continuation space, exhaustive comparison is available. Across unbounded decompositions, the finite characterization requires an additional argument.

The distinction connects usefully to PerfectJet’s exact representation work. A vector of sufficient boundary quantities should remain closed under every declared transfer. If it does not, the missing interaction is part of the returned mathematical diagnosis. In the present examples the binary population is insufficient for a specific higher-height question, and the span-two population supplies an explicit witness. This is an actual object-level result, stronger than merely observing that a chosen summary might omit information.

11.4 The relation to classical cut lattices

For a connected graph choose an orientation of its edges and write dd for the vertex-to-edge incidence map. Then EG(a)=∥da∥2E_G(a)=\|da\|^2, and kerd\ker d consists of common constant shifts. The image of integer vertex heights under dd is the integral cut lattice. Every integer height class modulo common shifts has a unique representative of minimum zero. Consequently

BG(1,q,1)=∑a∈ℤk/ℤ𝟏q∥da∥2 B_G(1,q,1)=\sum_{a\in\mathbb Z^k/\mathbb Z\mathbf1}q^{\|da\|^2}

is its ordinary theta series for 0<q<10<q<1. This is classical lattice territory. The relation between a cut lattice’s minimum norm and graph edge connectivity is established background [BHN1997]. Singularity’s elementary minimum-cut proof should be read as a proof in its chosen coordinates, not as a historical priority claim about that relationship.

The added volume and span markers retain the position of a height class relative to the vertex-height coordinate system. They are not invariants of an abstract Euclidean lattice by itself. An isometry of cut lattices need not preserve the minimum-normalized sum of vertex heights or their maximum. This is the precise sense in which the new object can distinguish vertex realizations that an ordinary theta series identifies.

The examples give a concrete instance. Gluing two graph blocks at a single vertex makes their cut lattices an orthogonal direct sum. To see this, independently choose integer heights on each block modulo constants, and shift their representatives so the common vertex agrees. The edge-energy sum splits into the two blocks, and the correspondence is bijective. A bridge contributes a one-dimensional standard integer lattice. Each spectral graph therefore has a cut lattice isometric to the triangle cut lattice plus four such bridge factors. Each binary graph has the cut lattice of its common theta block plus two bridge factors. The placement of those bridge attachments does not change this abstract lattice decomposition, but it does change the marked populations established in the preceding chapter.

This distinction also cautions against interpreting the construction as a new kind of Euclidean spectral statistic. The Laplacian spectrum, the abstract cut lattice, and the marked height population forget different information. Their comparison is valuable precisely because they are not interchangeable. The examples show a difference after some conventional data have been fixed; they do not prove a total ordering among every graph invariant.

11.5 Finite conductors and the part that is already old

The conductor archive studied rational phases and exact residue closure. The same algebraic mechanism works for the present unmarked local factor. Let q=ζLq=\zeta_L be an LL-th root of unity. Changing a single coordinate by LL changes energy by

EG(a+Lei)−EG(a)=2L∑j∼i(ai−aj)+L2di, E_G(a+Le_i)-E_G(a) =2L\sum_{j\sim i}(a_i-a_j)+L^2d_i,

which is divisible by LL. The phase is therefore periodic in each height coordinate modulo LL. Splitting ai=ri+Lbia_i=r_i+Lb_i gives the exact identity

PG(x,ζL)=NG,L(x)(1−xL)k,NG,L(x)=∑r∈{0,…,L−1}kζLEG(r)x|r|. P_G(x,\zeta_L)=\frac{N_{G,L}(x)}{(1-x^L)^k}, \qquad N_{G,L}(x)=\sum_{r\in\{0,\ldots,L-1\}^k} \zeta_L^{E_G(r)}x^{|r|}. \tag{SNG-I021}

The equality holds as a formal series and analytically for |x|<1|x|<1. It is a finite cyclotomic calculation. The archive already used this kind of residue decomposition for collision and Cartan quadratic forms [PJ2026]. Its presence here is an inherited bridge, not the new claim. The difference is that a graph Laplacian has a common-shift null direction and the project retains coordinate-sensitive marks around that direction.

The marked span variable prevents one from copying the same numerator formula unchanged. Adding LL to one coordinate can alter the common minimum and maximum, so its effect on the span marker is not determined by that coordinate’s residue alone. One may specialize to z=1z=1, keep a finite height cutoff, or develop an additional boundary description. The unmarked rational formula does not establish a correspondingly simple rational formula for the full marked series.

There is a further exact bridge to spanning trees. For an odd prime pp, let

ΓG(p)=∑a∈𝔽pkexp(2πiEG(a)/p). \Gamma_G(p)=\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_p^k} \exp\bigl(2\pi i E_G(a)/p\bigr).

Fix one vertex height to zero and separate the free common shift. The remaining quadratic form has a reduced Laplacian matrix with determinant τ(G)\tau(G), the spanning-tree count. If p∤τ(G)p\nmid\tau(G), the reduced form is nondegenerate. Standard finite-field diagonalization then gives

ΓG(p)=p(τ(G)p)gpk−1,gp=∑u∈𝔽pe2πiu2/p. \Gamma_G(p)=p\left(\frac{\tau(G)}p\right)g_p^{\,k-1}, \qquad g_p=\sum_{u\in\mathbb F_p}e^{2\pi i u^2/p}. \tag{SNG-I022}

In particular its absolute value is p(k+1)/2p^{(k+1)/2}. When pp divides the spanning-tree count, the reduced quadratic form is singular and this nondegenerate formula must be replaced by its rank-sensitive version, which holds for every graph, connected or not.

Theorem SNG-F30 (rank-sensitive Gauss sum). Let pp be an odd prime, ω=e2πi/p\omega=e^{2\pi i/p}, and gp=∑u∈𝔽pωu2g_p=\sum_{u\in\mathbb F_p}\omega^{u^2}. Let P∈GLk(𝔽p)P\in GL_k(\mathbb F_p) satisfy P⊤ΔGP≡diag(λ1,…,λr,0,…,0)P^{\top}\Delta_GP\equiv\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r,0,\ldots,0) with λi≢0\lambda_i\not\equiv0. Then rr is the rank of ΔG\Delta_G over 𝔽p\mathbb F_p, the class of D=λ1⋯λrD=\lambda_1\cdots\lambda_r modulo squares does not depend on PP, and ΓG(p)=pk−r(Dp)gpr, \Gamma_G(p)=p^{\,k-r}\left(\frac Dp\right)g_p^{\,r}, with the convention that the right side is pkp^k when r=0r=0.

Proof. Energy is the integer quadratic form a⊤ΔGaa^\top\Delta_Ga, so ωEG(a)\omega^{E_G(a)} depends only on amodpa\bmod p. Every symmetric matrix over a field of odd characteristic is congruent to a diagonal one: if some diagonal entry is nonzero, move it to the pivot and clear its row and column by the substitutions ej↦ej−(mkj/mkk)eke_j\mapsto e_j-(m_{kj}/m_{kk})e_k; if all remaining diagonal entries vanish but mij≠0m_{ij}\ne0, replace eie_i by ei+eje_i+e_j, whose new diagonal entry is 2mij≠02m_{ij}\ne0 because pp is odd; if the remaining block is zero, stop. Since PP is invertible, a=Pba=Pb is a bijection of 𝔽pk\mathbb F_p^k, so $$ \Gamma_G(p)=\sum_b\omega^{\sum_i\lambda_ib_i^2}=\prod_{i\le r}\Bigl(\sum_{u}\omega^{\lambda_iu^2}\Bigr)\cdot p^{\,k-r}. $$ Each zero diagonal entry is a singular direction and contributes a full factor pp; these include the constant vector of every connected component, and further directions at primes dividing invariant factors of the Laplacian. For λ≠0\lambda\ne0, substituting u↦λ−1uu\mapsto\lambda^{-1}u when λ\lambda is a square, and counting the solutions of u2=vu^2=v when it is not, gives ∑uωλu2=(λp)gp\sum_u\omega^{\lambda u^2}=\left(\frac\lambda p\right)g_p. Multiplicativity of the Legendre symbol gives the formula. Rank is a congruence invariant. The radical R=kerΔGR=\ker\Delta_G is intrinsic, and the induced nondegenerate form on 𝔽pk/R\mathbb F_p^k/R has Gram determinant DD in the basis given by the images of the first rr columns of PP. A change of basis multiplies it by a nonzero square, so the square class is well defined. ▫\square

For a connected graph with p∤τ(G)p\nmid\tau(G), the rank is k−1k-1 and DD has the square class of τ(G)\tau(G), which recovers SNG-I022. The triangle at p=3p=3 is an exceptional prime: τ=3\tau=3, and ΔK3≡2J(mod3)\Delta_{K_3}\equiv2J\pmod 3 has rank one, with D=2D=2 a non-square. Hence ΓK3(3)=−9g3=−9−18ω\Gamma_{K_3}(3)=-9g_3=-9-18\omega, whereas the nondegenerate formula would predict a multiple of g32g_3^2. The implementation src/singularity/gauss.py returns the diagonalizing matrix as a witness and rechecks P⊤ΔGPP^\top\Delta_GP and detP≠0\det P\ne0 exactly. It compares pk−r(D/p)gprp^{k-r}(D/p)g_p^r with the direct residue-cube sum in ℤ[t]/Φp(t)\mathbb Z[t]/\Phi_p(t), with no square root of pp, on all labeled graphs with at most four vertices for p=3,5,7p=3,5,7 and all five-vertex graphs for p=3p=3. It rejects p=2p=2, composite moduli and prime powers, which this theorem does not cover. This provides a defined arithmetic role for discriminant primes: they signal additional modular degeneracy. It does not make every finite-conductor phase statistic complete for graph reconstruction.

11.6 What the new direction actually adds

The archival programs often sought an invariant that survived a passage from a large object to a smaller representation. That ambition remains useful, but the present project asks a more relational inverse question: what is preserved when one counts every nested height pattern while forgetting which vertex carried it? A binary subset census counts one boundary at a time. A two-level height configuration simultaneously places two nested boundaries and records edges that cross both. The exact co-binary example proves that this added relation is not determined by the entire one-boundary census.

The difference should not be called a higher-body interaction in the energy. The energy remains a sum of pairwise edge terms. Higher relational information appears because the observation organizes those same pairwise terms across several nested threshold sets. This distinction matters both mathematically and historically.
